125298.m: The two annihilation photons fly off in opposite directions.

125299.q: How does a PET scanner recognise that two photons come from the same annihilation?
a: through coincidence measurement, meaning they arrive almost at the same time at opposite detectors
125299.e: Only photons that hit opposite detectors within a few nanoseconds are counted. The image is built up from many such lines.
125299.m: A PET scanner only counts photon pairs that arrive at the same time.

125300.q: With which method is PET often combined in one device to show metabolism and anatomy at the same time?
125300.e: PET shows where metabolism takes place, while CT provides exact images of the body’s structures. Together, findings can be located precisely.
125300.m: PET-CT combines an image of metabolism with anatomy.

125301.q: Which device is usually used to produce short-lived positron emitters such as fluorine-18?
125301.e: In a cyclotron, protons are accelerated and fired at a target material. This produces positron emitters such as fluorine-18.
125301.m: Positron emitters for PET usually come from a cyclotron.

125302.q: Why do many tumours show up well in PET with fluorodeoxyglucose?
a: because tumour cells take up a particularly large amount of sugar
because tumour cells take up no sugar
because tumours are colder than healthy tissue
125302.e: Many tumour cells have a high energy turnover and therefore take up a lot of labelled sugar. There, the tracer gives off particularly many positrons.
125302.m: Tumours with a high sugar consumption light up in PET.

125303.q: In which municipality in Aargau is the Paul Scherrer Institute mainly located?
125303.e: The institute lies on the Aare in Villigen and extends to Würenlingen. It is Switzerland’s largest research institute for natural and engineering sciences.
125303.m: The Paul Scherrer Institute is in Villigen in Aargau.

125304.q: Who was Paul Scherrer, after whom the research institute is named?
125304.e: Paul Scherrer headed the Institute of Physics at ETH Zurich for a long time. He did a great deal to promote nuclear physics in Switzerland.
125304.m: Paul Scherrer was an important physicist at ETH Zurich.

125305.q: To which group of institutions does the Paul Scherrer Institute belong?
125305.e: The ETH Domain includes the two Federal Institutes of Technology and four research institutes, among them PSI. It is funded by the federal government.
125305.m: The Paul Scherrer Institute belongs to the ETH Domain.

125306.q: What is the name of the Paul Scherrer Institute’s synchrotron light source?
125306.e: In the Swiss Light Source, electrons circle in a storage ring and produce very bright X-ray light. This is used to study materials and proteins.
125306.m: The Swiss Light Source produces intense synchrotron light at PSI.

125307.q: Which large facility at PSI produces extremely short and intense X-ray laser pulses?
125307.e: SwissFEL is a free-electron X-ray laser. With its ultra-short pulses, very fast processes in molecules can be observed.
125307.m: SwissFEL is the X-ray laser of the Paul Scherrer Institute.

125308.q: Which cancer treatment is offered at the Paul Scherrer Institute?
125308.e: At PSI, tumours are irradiated with protons, including eye tumours and tumours in children. Protons release their energy precisely at a certain depth.
125308.m: At the Paul Scherrer Institute, tumours are irradiated with protons.

125309.q: At PSI, muons are produced when fast protons hit a target. To which particle is the muon closely related?
125309.e: Like the electron, the muon is negatively charged, but about 200 times heavier. At PSI it is used as a tiny magnetic field probe in materials.
125309.m: The muon is a heavy relative of the electron.

125310.q: A cyclotron at PSI accelerates protons. What forces the protons onto their circular path?
125310.e: In a magnetic field, the Lorentz force acts on moving charges at right angles to their motion. It bends the protons onto a circular path, while an alternating electric field accelerates them further on each lap.
125310.m: In a cyclotron, a magnetic field keeps the particles on their circular path.

125311.q: PSI was formed in 1988 from two earlier institutes. Which field was central to both?
125311.e: The Federal Institute for Reactor Research (EIR) and the Swiss Institute for Nuclear Research (SIN) were merged in 1988. Today PSI also researches energy, materials and medicine.
125311.m: The Paul Scherrer Institute grew out of two nuclear research institutes.

125312.q: In composting, what is meant by “rotting” (Rotte)?
a: The aerobic breakdown of organic matter by microorganisms
The anaerobic fermentation of organic matter into methane
The chemical burning of green waste without a flame
The mechanical shredding of green waste before breakdown
125312.e: Rotting is a biological breakdown with access to air. Bacteria, fungi and small animals break down the organic matter.
125312.m: Rotting is a breakdown with oxygen.

125313.q: What is meant by windrow composting?
125313.e: A windrow is a long pile, usually with a triangular cross-section. This shape is common in larger composting plants because windrows can be turned by machine.
125313.m: Large composting plants often heap the material in long windrows.

125314.q: What is the cress test used for with compost?
a: It checks whether the compost is safe for plants
It measures the nitrogen content in per cent
It determines the temperature in the heap
It detects heavy metals in the compost
125314.e: You sow cress seeds on the compost and watch germination and growth. Unripe compost often contains substances that harm the seedlings.
125314.m: The cress test shows whether compost is safe for plants.

125315.q: Apart from humus, which substances mainly form during the aerobic breakdown of organic matter?
a: Hydrogen sulphide, ammonia and nitrous oxide
125315.e: Microorganisms respire the organic matter much as living things use their food. This releases carbon dioxide, water and lots of heat.
125315.m: Rotting produces carbon dioxide, water and heat.

125316.q: What does a rotten smell of hydrogen sulphide in a compost heap point to?
a: There is a lack of oxygen, often because it is too wet
The heap is too dry and too loose
Too many compost worms live in the heap
125316.e: Hydrogen sulphide forms during anaerobic rotting processes. Usually the heap is too wet or packed too tightly.
125316.m: A rotten smell shows a lack of oxygen in the compost.

125317.q: How can you tell that compost is ripe?
a: It hardly warms up any more and smells like forest soil
It gets hotter than 70 °C in the heap
It smells strongly of rotten eggs
You can still see all the leaves and peels
125317.e: In ripe compost, the easily broken-down matter has been used up, so hardly any heat is produced. It is dark, crumbly and smells like forest soil.
125317.m: Ripe compost is cool, crumbly and smells like forest soil.

125318.q: Which phase completes composting after the breakdown and conversion phases?
a: The build-up phase, in which stable humic substances form
The starting phase, in which sugar is broken down
The fermentation phase, in which methane forms
125318.e: In the build-up or maturing phase, the temperature drops and stable humic substances form. Now compost worms and other small animals also move in.
125318.m: At the end of composting, stable humic substances form.

125319.q: Which microorganisms cause the typical forest-soil smell of ripe compost?
125319.e: Actinomycetes produce the scent geosmin. It smells of fresh forest soil and shows that compost has rotted well.
125319.m: Actinomycetes give compost the smell of forest soil.

125320.q: In which temperature range does the thermophilic phase of composting typically lie?
125320.e: In hot rotting, well-built heaps reach about 50 to 70 °C. This phase lasts from a few days to weeks, depending on the material.
125320.m: In hot rotting, compost gets about 50 to 70 °C warm.

125321.q: What benefit does the thermophilic phase have for compost quality?
a: Pathogens and weed seeds are killed
The compost is enriched with nitrogen from the air
Heavy metals are completely broken down
125321.e: The high temperatures sanitise the compost. Weed seeds that could germinate and many pathogens do not survive this heat.
125321.m: The heat in compost kills germs and weed seeds.

125322.q: Where are compost worms in a compost heap during hot rotting?
a: In the cooler edges and at the bottom
In the hottest core of the heap
They survive hot rotting inside as eggs
125322.e: Compost worms cannot stand the high temperatures in the core. They move to cooler zones and only move back into the heap after it has cooled down.
125322.m: Compost worms avoid the hot core of the compost.

125323.q: Which phase comes before the thermophilic phase in composting?
125323.e: At the start, mesophilic microorganisms multiply at medium temperatures. The heat from their metabolism gradually warms up the heap.
125323.m: The mesophilic phase is followed by the thermophilic phase.

125324.q: What does the technical term “thermophilic” mean?
125324.e: The term comes from Greek: thermos means warm, philos means loving. Cold-loving organisms are called psychrophilic.

125325.q: Why does a very small compost heap often not reach a thermophilic phase?
a: It loses too much heat through its surface compared with its mass
It always contains too much oxygen
It has too narrow a C/N ratio
125325.e: In small heaps, the surface is large compared with the volume. The heat produced escapes faster than it is made.
125325.m: Small compost heaps cool down too quickly.

125326.q: Why are temperatures well above 70 °C unwanted in compost?
a: Useful microorganisms die too and breakdown slows down
The compost then starts to freeze
Methane is then bound to form
The plant nutrients turn into metals
125326.e: Very high temperatures harm most of the organisms that do the breaking down. The process slows down, and more nitrogen is lost as ammonia.
125326.m: Too much heat slows down rotting.

125327.q: Which organisms dominate in the thermophilic phase of composting?
125327.e: Above 50 °C, mainly thermophilic bacteria and actinomycetes survive. Small animals such as worms avoid the hot zone.
125327.m: In the heat, mainly bacteria and actinomycetes are at work.

125328.q: Which C/N ratio is considered good for the starting material of a compost?
125328.e: Microorganisms need carbon as an energy source and nitrogen to build their proteins. A ratio of about 25 to 30 to 1 allows quick breakdown.
125328.m: A good compost start has a C/N ratio of about 25 to 30 to 1.

125329.q: Roughly what C/N ratio does ripe compost have?
125329.e: During rotting, a lot of carbon escapes as carbon dioxide. Ripe compost therefore has a similarly narrow C/N ratio to humus in the soil.
125329.m: Ripe compost has a narrow C/N ratio.

125330.q: Which material provides a compost with especially large amounts of nitrogen?
125330.e: Fresh green plant material is rich in protein and therefore in nitrogen. Leaves, straw and branches mainly add carbon.
125330.m: Fresh green material brings nitrogen into the compost.

125331.q: What happens if the C/N ratio in compost is too narrow?
a: Nitrogen escapes as ammonia and it smells sharp
Breakdown almost stops because of a lack of nitrogen
The compost never gets warmer than 15 °C
125331.e: If there is too much nitrogen, the microorganisms cannot use all of it. The rest is lost as ammonia.
125331.m: Too much nitrogen escapes as ammonia.

125332.q: What happens if the C/N ratio in compost is too wide?
a: Breakdown is slow because nitrogen is lacking
The compost smells strongly of ammonia
The compost immediately turns into humus
125332.e: Microorganisms need nitrogen for their growth. If it is lacking, they hardly multiply and the material breaks down only slowly.
125332.m: If nitrogen is lacking, material rots only slowly.

125333.q: A compost mixture contains 15 kg of carbon and 0.5 kg of nitrogen. What is its C/N ratio?
125333.e: You divide the mass of carbon by the mass of nitrogen: 15 kg ÷ 0.5 kg gives 30. So the ratio is 30 to 1.
125333.m: The C/N ratio is the mass of carbon divided by the mass of nitrogen.

125334.q: You mix material with 30 kg C and 0.5 kg N with material with 10 kg C and 1 kg N. What C/N ratio does the mixture have?
125334.e: You add the masses: 30 + 10 gives 40 kg C, 0.5 + 1 gives 1.5 kg N. 40 ÷ 1.5 gives about 26.7, so about 27 to 1. You must not simply average the individual ratios.
125334.m: For mixtures, you calculate with the total masses of C and N.

125335.q: Why can straw freshly worked into the soil cause a temporary nitrogen shortage in plants?
a: Microorganisms take nitrogen from the soil to break down the straw
Straw releases nitrogen as nitrous oxide when it breaks down
Straw stops rain from getting into the soil
Straw contains substances that kill roots immediately
125335.e: Straw has a very wide C/N ratio. The microorganisms breaking it down build nitrogen from the soil into their cells, so the plants lack it for a while.
125335.m: Breaking down straw can temporarily lock up nitrogen in the soil.

125336.q: How can you improve a compost heap that consists almost only of fresh grass clippings?
a: By mixing in carbon-rich, coarse shredded material
By adding even more grass clippings
By pressing the material down firmly
By covering it with an airtight sheet
125336.e: Grass clippings are rich in nitrogen and easily collapse. Shredded material provides carbon and creates spaces for air.
125336.m: Grass clippings need coarse, carbon-rich material as a partner.

125337.q: Which flammable gas mainly forms when green waste is fermented in a biogas plant?
125337.e: Biogas consists of about half to two thirds methane; the rest is mainly carbon dioxide. The methane can be turned into electricity, heat or fuel.

125338.q: With which step does the multi-stage breakdown in fermentation begin?
125338.e: In hydrolysis, enzymes split large molecules such as proteins, fats and carbohydrates into small building blocks. Only then do acidification, acetic acid formation and methane formation follow.

125339.q: Which group of organisms forms the methane in the last step of fermentation?
125339.e: Methane producers belong to the archaea, a separate domain of life. They make methane mainly from acetic acid or from hydrogen and carbon dioxide.

125340.q: Why must the digester in a biogas plant be sealed airtight?
a: Methane producers only work without oxygen
Otherwise the water escapes as steam
Otherwise the green waste turns into crude oil
125340.e: Fermentation is an anaerobic process. If oxygen gets in, the material is composted instead of fermented, and no methane forms.

125341.q: What is typical of dry fermentation compared with wet fermentation?
a: The substrate has a higher dry matter content
The process takes place with oxygen
125341.e: In dry fermentation, the material can be stacked or is paste-like. In wet fermentation, it can be pumped like slurry.
125341.m: Dry fermentation works with firmer material than wet fermentation.

125342.q: What is an important advantage of fermenting green waste compared with composting alone?
a: Besides fertiliser, energy is gained as biogas
No residues are produced at all
It needs neither containers nor technology
The green waste is turned into crude oil
125342.e: In composting, the energy is lost as heat. In fermentation, it stays stored in the methane and can be used.
125342.m: Fermentation provides energy and fertiliser at the same time.

125343.q: What happens if a digester is overfed with too much easily broken-down material?
a: Organic acids build up and the pH value drops
125343.e: The acid-forming bacteria work faster than the methane producers. If the acids build up, the pH value drops and methane production collapses.

125344.q: In which pH range do methane producers work best?
125344.e: Methane-producing archaea are sensitive to acids. A nearly neutral pH value is ideal.
125344.m: Methane producers like a neutral pH value.

125345.q: What happens in a biogas plant to gas that cannot be used, for example when an engine breaks down?
a: It is burnt in an emergency flare
It is released unused into the air
It is pumped into the ground
125345.e: Methane should not get into the atmosphere unburnt. The emergency flare turns it into carbon dioxide, which harms the climate less.
125345.m: Surplus biogas is burnt in a flare.

125346.q: Roughly how much methane does raw biogas contain?
125346.e: Raw biogas typically contains about 50 to 75 per cent methane. Only after upgrading does almost pure biomethane result.
125346.m: Raw biogas is about half to three quarters methane.

125347.q: What job does the stirrer in the digester of a biogas plant do?
a: It mixes the substrate and prevents floating layers
It produces the electricity by friction
It supplies oxygen to the digester
It grinds the digestate into powder
125347.e: Stirring brings microorganisms and substrate into contact, and the heat spreads evenly. Gas bubbles are also released more easily.
125347.m: Stirrers keep the contents of the digester moving.

125348.q: Why is the digester of a biogas plant usually heated?
a: The microorganisms work best at a constant, warm temperature
So that the substrate starts to boil
So that the biogas becomes liquid
125348.e: Changes in temperature disturb the sensitive methane producers. That is why part of the waste heat from the combined heat and power unit is used to heat the digester.
125348.m: Digesters are kept at an even temperature.

125349.q: What mainly has to be removed when upgrading biogas to biomethane?
125349.e: By removing carbon dioxide and trace gases, the gas reaches natural gas quality. It can then be fed into the gas network.
125349.m: For biomethane, the carbon dioxide is removed.

125350.q: Why is sulphur removed from biogas before it is used in an engine?
a: Hydrogen sulphide is corrosive and damages the engine
Sulphur raises the methane content too much
Sulphur turns the gas a poisonous green
125350.e: When it burns, hydrogen sulphide forms sulphurous acid. This attacks metal parts and shortens the life of the engines.
125350.m: Sulphur is removed from biogas to protect engines.

125351.q: A digester holds 2,000 m³ and receives 50 m³ of substrate every day. How long does the substrate stay in it on average?
125351.e: The average retention time is the digester volume divided by the daily input. 2,000 m³ ÷ 50 m³ per day gives 40 days.
125351.m: Retention time is the volume divided by the daily input.

125352.q: Why is slurry often fermented together with other substrates in biogas plants?
a: Slurry alone gives relatively little gas, because the animals have already taken much of its energy
Slurry alone would make the digester explode
Slurry contains no organic matter at all
Slurry may not be fermented on its own in Switzerland
125352.e: During digestion, the animals have already used most of the energy-rich substances. Co-substrates such as food waste or green waste increase the gas yield a lot.
125352.m: Co-substrates increase the gas yield from slurry.

125353.q: Why is the gas from old landfill sites collected instead of being allowed to escape?
a: It contains a lot of methane, a strong greenhouse gas
125353.e: In landfills, microorganisms break down organic waste without air. The landfill gas produced contains lots of methane, which is burnt or used to produce energy.
125353.m: Landfill gas contains methane, which harms the climate.

125354.q: What happens to nutrients such as nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium during fermentation?
a: Most of them stay in the digestate
They all pass into the biogas
They turn into methane in the digester
They disappear because of the heat
125354.e: The biogas mainly takes up carbon, hydrogen and oxygen. The plant nutrients stay in the digestate and go back onto the fields with it.
125354.m: The nutrients stay in the digestate.

125355.q: What is liquid digestate usually used for after separation?
a: As liquid fertiliser on meadows and fields
As drinking water for farm animals
As coolant in the combined heat and power unit
125355.e: In separation, digestate is divided into a solid and a liquid part. The liquid part is spread as fertiliser, like slurry.
125355.m: Liquid digestate is a liquid fertiliser.

125356.q: Why is nitrogen in digestate quickly available to plants?
a: A large part of it is in the form of ammonium
It is firmly bound in wood fibres
It is pure nitrogen from the air
It is locked up in biochar
125356.e: During fermentation, proteins are broken down and the nitrogen is released as ammonium. Plants can take up this form quickly.
125356.m: Digestate contains lots of quickly available ammonium.

125357.q: How can ammonia losses be reduced when spreading liquid digestate?
a: By spreading it close to the ground, for example with trailing hoses
By spraying it in a wide arc in sunshine
By spreading it on frozen ground
125357.e: The less contact the liquid has with the air, the less ammonia escapes. Trailing hoses lay the digestate directly on the ground.
125357.m: Spreading close to the ground saves nitrogen.

125358.q: Why does digestate usually contribute less to humus formation than compost?
a: Part of the carbon has already been removed as biogas
It is always burnt before going onto the field
125358.e: During fermentation, easily broken-down carbon goes into methane and carbon dioxide. Less organic matter is therefore left in the digestate for building up humus.
125358.m: Compost builds up more humus than digestate.

125359.q: What is the purpose of post-composting solid digestate?
a: It is turned into stable compost with access to air
It is fermented into biogas again
125359.e: Solid digestate can be composted aerobically afterwards, like green waste. This produces a ripe compost that keeps well.
125359.m: Post-composting turns solid digestate into compost.

125360.q: Why do ordinary plastic bags not belong in green waste for fermentation?
a: They end up in the digestate as foreign matter and microplastics
They raise the methane content dangerously
125360.e: Plastics are not broken down in the plant. If they are not sieved out, bits of plastic end up on the fields with the fertiliser.
125360.m: Plastic in green waste pollutes the fertiliser.

125361.q: Why does fermented slurry usually smell less strongly than unfermented slurry?
a: Many strong-smelling organic acids have been broken down
Perfume has been added to it
125361.e: In the digester, volatile fatty acids are largely converted into methane. These acids contribute a lot to the smell of slurry.
125361.m: Fermentation reduces the smell of slurry.

125362.q: By which process is biochar made?
a: By pyrolysis with very little oxygen
125362.e: Biomass is heated strongly with no or very little oxygen. It does not burn but turns into charcoal.

125363.q: Which property makes biochar especially interesting for soils?
a: Its very large inner surface thanks to many pores
Its fast breakdown within a few days
125363.e: Because of its pore structure, even one gram of biochar has a huge surface area. This can hold water and nutrients and be colonised by microorganisms.
125363.m: Biochar is porous and stores water and nutrients.

125364.q: Why is biochar in the soil considered a carbon sink?
a: Its carbon is broken down only very slowly
It takes up methane as it rots
It turns carbon dioxide directly into oxygen
It keeps slowly burning in the soil
125364.e: The carbon in biochar is in very stable ring structures. It therefore stays in the soil for a long time instead of getting into the air as carbon dioxide.
125364.m: Biochar stores carbon in the soil for a long time.

125365.q: Why should biochar be loaded with nutrients before it is worked into the soil?
a: Otherwise fresh char would bind nutrients from the soil
Otherwise it would explode in the soil
Otherwise it would make the soil freeze
125365.e: Unloaded biochar soaks up nutrients like a sponge. If you first mix it with compost or slurry, it later releases them to plants.
125365.m: Biochar is loaded with nutrients before use.

125366.q: What is the technical term for charcoal made from biomass for use in soil?
125366.e: Biochar is made up of “bio” and “char” for something charred. The term stresses its use in soil rather than as a fuel.
125366.m: Charcoal for soil is called biochar.

125367.q: What usually happens to the pyrolysis gases produced in modern pyrolysis plants?
a: They are burnt and provide process or heating energy
They are released unused into the air
They are condensed into drinking water
They are pressed into the ground
125367.e: The flammable gases from the biomass are burnt in a combustion chamber. The heat keeps the pyrolysis going and can also be used for heating.
125367.m: Pyrolysis gases provide heat for the plant.

125368.q: What is the main difference between biochar and barbecue charcoal?
a: Its use and the quality requirements for soils
It is made from crude oil instead of wood
It contains no carbon at all
It is burnt with plenty of oxygen
125368.e: Both are made by charring biomass. But biochar for soil must meet strict limits, for example for pollutants.
125368.m: Biochar is charcoal for the soil rather than for the barbecue.

125369.q: How is biochar often used in livestock farming?
a: As a feed additive to support digestion
As fuel to heat the animals
As a replacement for drinking water
125369.e: Small amounts of feed charcoal are mixed into the feed. Through the manure, the charcoal later also gets into the soil.
125369.m: Biochar can be used as a feed additive.

125370.q: In which region has terra preta mainly been found?
125370.e: Terra preta is found in patches in Amazonia, often along rivers. Larger settlements used to exist there.
125370.m: Terra preta comes from the Amazon region.

125371.q: What does the Portuguese expression “terra preta” mean?
125371.e: The name describes the strikingly dark colour of these soils. They are clearly different from the light, reddish or yellowish soils around them.

125372.q: How did terra preta come about?
a: Through human settlement with charcoal and waste
Through volcanic eruptions in the rainforest
Through glaciers in the last Ice Age
125372.e: Terra preta is a man-made soil. Charcoal, kitchen waste and faeces built up near settlements over a long time.
125372.m: Terra preta is soil made by people.

125373.q: Which finds are typical of terra preta soils and show that they were made by people?
125373.e: Terra preta often contains many pottery shards. They prove that people lived there and left their waste.
125373.m: Pottery shards reveal the human origin of terra preta.

125374.q: What are the natural soils in the Amazon region usually like?
a: Heavily weathered and poor in nutrients
Very rich in humus and deep black
125374.e: High temperatures and heavy rainfall wash out nutrients. Many rainforest soils are therefore poor despite the lush vegetation.
125374.m: Many rainforest soils are poor in nutrients.

125375.q: Why are researchers interested in terra preta today?
a: As a model for soils with biochar
Because it contains a lot of gold
As a building material for houses
125375.e: The charcoal in terra preta stays in the soil for centuries, holds on to nutrients and stores carbon. Today people are trying to create similarly fertile soils with biochar.
125375.m: Terra preta is a model for soils with biochar.

125376.q: Who made most terra preta soils?
125376.e: The soils formed long before the Europeans arrived. They show that larger settled communities once lived in the Amazon region.
125376.m: Terra preta dates from pre-Columbian times.

125377.q: Which waste contributed most to the high phosphorus content of terra preta?
125377.e: Bones and fish bones contain a lot of calcium phosphate. Over a long time, their remains enriched the soil with phosphorus.
125377.m: Bone remains made terra preta rich in phosphorus.

125378.q: Which country does the bokashi method come from?
125378.e: The word bokashi is Japanese. It means fermented organic material.

125379.q: Which process mainly takes place in a bokashi bucket?
a: Hot composting with lots of oxygen
125379.e: Lactic acid bacteria ferment the kitchen waste without air. It is a fermentation, not a rotting process.
125379.m: Bokashi is a lactic acid fermentation.

125380.q: Which mixture of microorganisms is often used for bokashi?
125380.e: Effective microorganisms are a mixture mainly of lactic acid bacteria, yeasts and photosynthetic bacteria. They are sprayed over the waste or added as inoculated bran.
125380.m: Effective microorganisms are often used for bokashi.

125381.q: What is the tap at the bottom of a bokashi bucket for?
125381.e: Liquid comes out during fermentation. It has to be drained off regularly so that the waste does not rot.
125381.m: The liquid is drained off at the bottom of the bokashi bucket.

125382.q: How is the liquid from a bokashi bucket used in the garden?
a: Heavily diluted as a liquid fertiliser
Undiluted as drinking water for birds
As a replacement for potting compost
125382.e: The liquid contains nutrients and microorganisms. It is acidic and is therefore heavily diluted before watering.
125382.m: Bokashi liquid is used diluted as fertiliser.

125383.q: What does successful bokashi smell like?
125383.e: The lactic acid produced gives a sour smell. A rotten smell suggests that rotting bacteria have taken over.

125384.q: What has to happen to fully fermented bokashi for humus to form?
a: It has to be buried in soil or composted
It has to be dried and burnt
It has to be put in the fridge
It has to be dissolved in water and poured away
125384.e: Fermented bokashi is pre-digested but not yet decomposed material. Only in the soil do soil organisms turn it into humus within a few weeks.
125384.m: Bokashi only becomes humus in the soil.

125385.q: Why does the waste in a bokashi bucket normally not rot?
a: The lactic acid produced lowers the pH value and holds back rotting bacteria
The bucket is constantly heated above 70 °C
The waste is preserved with salt
There is too much oxygen in the bucket
125385.e: The lactic acid makes the conditions acidic. Rotting bacteria can hardly grow in these acidic conditions, much like in silage.
125385.m: The acid protects bokashi from rotting.

125386.q: What is the easiest way to separate compost worms from finished worm compost?
a: You put fresh food on one side, and the worms move there
You sieve everything at high heat
You rinse the worms out with salt water
125386.e: Compost worms follow the fresh food. The ripe worm compost on the other side is then almost free of worms and can be taken out.
125386.m: Fresh food lures worms out of finished worm compost.

125387.q: What is the product of worm composting called?
125387.e: The worms eat organic waste and excrete nutrient-rich crumbs. This worm compost is considered a high-quality fertiliser.

125388.q: What is the technical term for composting with worms?
125388.e: The term comes from the Latin word vermis for worm. It describes how worms and microorganisms turn organic waste into compost.
125388.m: Worm composting is also called vermicomposting.

125389.q: Which worm species is used most often in wormeries?
125389.e: The brandling worm multiplies quickly and eats large amounts of organic waste. Deep-burrowing species such as the common earthworm are not suitable for a wormery.
125389.m: Wormeries usually use the brandling worm Eisenia fetida.

125390.q: Which disadvantage results from the fact that worm compost does not get hot?
a: Weed seeds and pathogens are not reliably killed
A great deal of methane is produced
The worm compost contains no nutrients
The material does not rot at all
125390.e: Without a thermophilic phase, there is no sanitisation. Weed seeds can still germinate from worm compost.
125390.m: Worm compost is not sanitised by heat.

125391.q: Why must the material in a wormery always be moist?
a: Worms breathe through their moist skin
Worms turn dry material into stone
125391.e: Earthworms and compost worms have no lungs. Gas exchange happens through the skin, which must be moist for this.

125392.q: Which waste should not be put in a wormery?
125392.e: Meat and bones attract pests and rot easily. Plant-based kitchen waste and a little paper, on the other hand, are well suited.
125392.m: Meat does not belong in a wormery.

125393.q: In which soil layer does the brandling worm naturally live?
a: In the top litter layer with rotting material
In rock crevices without organic material
125393.e: Brandling worms live where leaves, manure and other organic remains lie. They do not dig deep, vertical tunnels like some other earthworms.
125393.m: The brandling worm lives in the top, organic layer.

125394.q: Which fuel is used in many wood-fired district heating plants in Switzerland?
125394.e: Wood chips are chopped from forest wood, leftover wood or wood from landscape maintenance. They are well suited for large, automatically fed boilers.
125394.m: Wood-fired district heating often runs on wood chips.

125395.q: Which biomass energy source is the most important in Switzerland?
125395.e: Switzerland has a lot of forest, and energy wood is used for heating and district heating. Wood is therefore the country’s most important energy source from biomass.
125395.m: Wood is Switzerland’s most important biomass energy.

125396.q: Which wood component is hard to break down and makes producing ethanol from wood difficult?
125396.e: Lignin makes cell walls woody and wraps around the cellulose. It must first be broken open before enzymes can break the cellulose down into sugar.
125396.m: Lignin makes wood hard to ferment.

125397.q: By which process is bioethanol produced?
a: By alcoholic fermentation of sugar or starch with yeasts
125397.e: Yeasts turn sugar into ethanol and carbon dioxide without air. Then the ethanol is separated by distillation.
125397.m: Bioethanol is produced by alcoholic fermentation.

125398.q: How is biodiesel made from vegetable oil such as rapeseed oil?
a: By fermentation with lactic acid bacteria
125398.e: In transesterification, the fats react with methanol to form fatty acid methyl esters. Glycerol is produced as a by-product.
125398.m: Biodiesel is made by transesterification of vegetable oil.

125399.q: Which problem does the “food or fuel” debate describe?
a: Energy crops compete with food for farmland
Cars use more electricity than kitchen appliances
Petrol stations sell too much food
Plates made of bioplastic are too expensive
125399.e: If grain or maize is turned into fuel, this land is missing for feeding people. This can affect food prices.

125400.q: Where does the energy stored in biomass originally come from?
a: From geothermal heat deep inside the Earth
From nuclear fission in the ground
125400.e: Plants convert sunlight into chemical energy and store it in sugar, starch and cellulose. This energy is released again when it is burnt.

125401.q: Which environmental disadvantage is especially linked with small wood-burning stoves?
125401.e: When wood is not burnt completely, many fine soot particles form. Lighting the fire properly and using dry wood reduce fine particles.
125401.m: Wood fires can produce a lot of fine particulate matter.

125402.q: Why should firewood be dried well before burning?
a: Evaporating water uses up energy and increases smoke
Dry wood contains more carbon atoms
Wet wood explodes in the stove
125402.e: Damp wood gives less usable heat, because part of the energy goes into evaporating the water. It also burns less completely and produces more soot.
125402.m: Dry wood burns more cleanly and gives more heat.

125403.q: What problem arises when PLA bottles end up in the PET collection?
a: They dissolve immediately in the collection bag
125403.e: PLA and PET look similar but have different properties. Even small amounts of PLA can lower the quality of the recycled PET.
125403.m: PLA does not belong in the PET collection.

125404.q: What is true of bio-based plastics?
a: They always break down in the garden within days
They are always made from crude oil
They are always soluble in water
125404.e: Bio-based describes the raw material, biodegradable describes what happens at the end. A plastic made from plants can be very durable.
125404.m: Bio-based does not automatically mean biodegradable.

125405.q: Which bio-based plastic is chemically identical to ordinary polyethylene and is not biodegradable?
125405.e: For bio-PE, ethanol is made from sugar cane, and ethene is made from that. The polyethylene formed from it behaves like polyethylene made from crude oil.
125405.m: Bio-PE is bio-based but not biodegradable.

125406.q: Which bioplastics are made by bacteria as storage substances?
125406.e: Certain bacteria store PHA as an energy reserve when nutrients are scarce. These plastics are bio-based and biodegradable.
125406.m: PHA are plastics that bacteria make themselves.

125407.q: Under which conditions does PLA usually break down well?
a: In industrial composting plants at high temperatures
In cold sea water within days
On its own in dry desert sand
In a home compost heap at winter temperatures
125407.e: To break down quickly, PLA needs heat and moisture as in hot composting. In nature or in a cool garden compost heap, it decomposes only very slowly.
125407.m: PLA needs heat to break down.

125408.q: What does the label “industrially compostable” on packaging mean?
a: It only breaks down quickly under the conditions of a composting plant
It breaks down in any garden compost within days
It is definitely not made of plastic
It can go in the PET collection
125408.e: To break down quickly, it needs heat and moisture as in a composting plant. In a cool garden compost heap or in nature, the material decomposes only very slowly.
125408.m: Industrially compostable does not mean compostable in the garden.

125409.q: Why do some Swiss municipalities not allow compostable plastic bags in green waste?
a: They can hardly be told apart from ordinary plastic bags
They contain too much nitrogen for rotting
They colour the finished compost dark
They count as hazardous waste by law
125409.e: Each municipality sets its own rules for green waste. Experience shows that where such bags are allowed, more ordinary plastic bags, which do not break down, also end up in the green waste.
125409.m: Each municipality decides whether compostable bags may go in green waste.

125410.q: Which early plastic was made from cellulose?
125410.e: Celluloid is made from cellulose nitrate and camphor and was used, among other things, for films. Bakelite, nylon and Teflon are made from fossil raw materials.
125410.m: Celluloid is an early plastic made from cellulose.

125411.q: What is thermoplastic starch, a common bioplastic, made of?
a: Starch processed with plasticisers such as glycerol
125411.e: Starch from potatoes or maize is broken open with plasticisers under heat and pressure. Then it can be shaped like a plastic.
125411.m: Thermoplastic starch is starch that can be shaped.

125510.q: What is the WHO's international classification system called, in which depression is also described as an illness?
125510.e: The ICD (International Classification of Diseases) is the diagnostic system of the World Health Organization. The DSM, by contrast, comes from the American Psychiatric Association.
125510.m: The ICD is the WHO's list of diseases.

125511.q: According to ICD-10, which feature is one of the main symptoms of depression?
a: Greatly increased need for sleep after sport
125511.e: The main symptoms include low mood, loss of interest and enjoyment, and reduced drive. Increased drive and ideas of grandeur are more typical of mania.
125511.m: Loss of enjoyment is a core symptom of depression.

125512.q: What does the technical term “anhedonia” mean?
a: Restlessness in the legs while sleeping
125512.e: Anhedonia comes from Greek and means roughly “without pleasure or joy”. It is a common symptom of depression.
125512.m: Anhedonia means you can no longer feel pleasure.

125513.q: According to ICD-10, how long must the symptoms last at least for a depressive episode to be diagnosed?
125513.e: For a depressive episode, ICD-10 requires a duration of at least about two weeks. Short phases of sadness are not yet depression.
125513.m: A depressive episode lasts at least about two weeks.

125514.q: What is the mental illness called in which depressive and manic phases alternate?
125514.e: In bipolar disorder, phases of low mood alternate with phases of exaggerated mood and activity. It used to be called manic depression.
125514.m: In bipolar disorder, depression and mania alternate.

125515.q: What is a chronic, milder depressive low mood that lasts for years called?
125515.e: Dysthymia is a lasting but less severe depressive low mood over at least two years. Cyclothymia, by contrast, is a mild form of changing moods.
125515.m: Dysthymia is a long-lasting mild depression.

125516.q: Which messenger substance in the brain do the commonly prescribed SSRI antidepressants mainly act on?
125516.e: SSRI stands for “selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors”. They prevent serotonin from being quickly taken back into the nerve cell.
125516.m: SSRIs act on the messenger substance serotonin.

125517.q: Which treatment is often used for seasonal affective disorder (“winter depression”)?
125517.e: In winter depression, the lack of light in the dark season plays a role. Bright light from special lamps can ease the symptoms.
125517.m: Light therapy often helps against winter depression.

125518.q: When does the mood-lifting effect of antidepressants typically begin?
a: Often only after a few weeks
125518.e: Antidepressants usually work with a delay, often only after two to four weeks. That is why patience is important, and you should not stop taking them on your own.
125518.m: Antidepressants usually only work after a few weeks.

a: Fear of only one particular animal
Fear of being judged by others
125519.e: In panic disorder, panic attacks happen again and again, apparently for no reason. Often a fear of the next attack develops as well.
125519.m: Panic disorder shows itself through repeated unexpected panic attacks.

125520.q: What are people with agoraphobia typically afraid of?
a: Places from which escape seems difficult
125520.e: Agoraphobia originally means “fear of the marketplace”. People fear crowds, public transport or places where help or escape seems difficult.
125520.m: People with agoraphobia avoid places that would be hard to escape from.

125521.q: Which anxiety disorder is mainly characterised by fear of being judged by other people?
125521.e: In social phobia, people fear embarrassing themselves or being judged negatively. Situations such as giving talks or conversations are therefore often avoided.
125521.m: Social phobia is the fear of being judged negatively by others.

125522.q: What is typical of generalised anxiety disorder?
a: Lasting worries about many areas of life
125522.e: In generalised anxiety disorder, thoughts revolve around many everyday worries for months. Tension, restlessness and sleep problems are often added.
125522.m: In generalised anxiety disorder, you constantly worry about many things.

125523.q: What is the abnormal fear of narrow, enclosed spaces called?
125523.e: Claustrophobia comes from the Latin “claustrum”, meaning “a closed place”. People affected avoid lifts or narrow tubes, for example.
125523.m: Claustrophobia is the fear of enclosed spaces.

125524.q: Which method is considered particularly effective for specific phobias?
125524.e: In exposure therapy, you face the feared situation step by step with support. You learn that the fear goes down again by itself.
125524.m: For phobias, gradually facing the fear helps.

125525.q: Which part of the nervous system triggers typical physical reactions to fear, such as a racing heart and sweating?
125525.e: The sympathetic nervous system prepares the body for fight or flight. Heartbeat and breathing speed up, and you sweat.
125525.m: The sympathetic nervous system controls the fight-or-flight response.

125526.q: Why does avoidance behaviour strengthen a fear in the long run?
a: You never experience that the danger does not happen
You move too little in everyday life
It makes you sleep too much
It makes you eat too much sugar
125526.e: Avoiding a situation brings short-term relief. But you never find out that what you fear does not happen, so the fear remains.
125526.m: Avoidance brings brief relief but keeps the fear alive.

125527.q: How does the WHO classify burnout in ICD-11?
a: As a psychosis in its own right
125527.e: In ICD-11, burnout appears as a phenomenon linked to work, not as a medical illness in its own right. It is explicitly related to chronic stress at the workplace.
125527.m: The WHO describes burnout as a result of chronic stress at work.

125528.q: Which dimension is one of Christina Maslach's three core features of burnout?
125528.e: Maslach describes emotional exhaustion, a detached attitude and reduced performance. Exhaustion is considered the central feature.
125528.m: Emotional exhaustion is a core feature of burnout.

125529.q: What is the well-known questionnaire for measuring burnout called?
125529.e: The Maslach Burnout Inventory (MBI) was developed by Christina Maslach and colleagues. It is used in research all over the world.
125529.m: The Maslach Burnout Inventory measures burnout.

125530.q: Which psychologist coined the term “burnout” in the 1970s?
125530.e: In the 1970s, the psychologist Herbert Freudenberger described the exhaustion of people in helping roles. In doing so, he made the term known in psychology.
125530.m: Herbert Freudenberger made the term burnout known.

125531.q: What does “depersonalisation” mean in Maslach's burnout model?
a: A detached, indifferent attitude towards others
125531.e: It means a cynical, numbed attitude towards clients, patients or colleagues. It often serves as protection against being overwhelmed further.
125531.m: With burnout, people often become detached and cynical.

125532.q: In which professions was burnout originally described above all?
125532.e: The first descriptions concerned people in nursing, social work and counselling. Today we know that burnout can occur in all professions.
125532.m: Burnout was first described in caring professions.

125533.q: According to the job demands-resources model, when does the risk of burnout rise particularly?
125533.e: The model distinguishes stressful demands from supporting resources such as freedom to make decisions or support. If resources are lacking under high strain, the risk rises.
125533.m: High strain and little support encourage burnout.

125534.q: Which measure is considered important for preventing burnout?
a: Being available on your mobile at all times
125534.e: Breaks, holidays, sleep and a clear separation of work and free time help to rebuild strength. Social support also protects.
125534.m: Recovery and clear boundaries protect against burnout.

a: Too little exercise in everyday life
125535.e: PTSD develops after a traumatic experience such as a serious accident, war, violence or a natural disaster. Not everyone who experiences a trauma develops PTSD.

125536.q: What is the sudden, unwanted reliving of a trauma as if it were happening right now called?
125536.e: In a flashback, images, sounds or feelings of the trauma come back very vividly. Experts also speak of intrusions.
125536.m: A flashback is an unwanted reliving of the trauma.

125537.q: In PTSD, what is meant by “hyperarousal”?
a: Lasting overexcitement and being easily startled
125537.e: Hyperarousal means the body is constantly on alert. Those affected sleep badly, are irritable and startle easily.
125537.m: In PTSD, the body often stays on alert.

125538.q: Which therapy method for PTSD uses targeted eye movements?
125538.e: EMDR stands for “Eye Movement Desensitization and Reprocessing” and was developed by Francine Shapiro. Memories are processed with the help of eye movements.
125538.m: EMDR is a trauma therapy using eye movements.

125539.q: Which English term was used in the First World War for the psychological effects of war on soldiers?
125539.e: “Shell shock” refers to the shock of exploding shells. Many of the symptoms described at that time would be classed as PTSD today.
125539.m: Shell shock was an early name for war trauma.

125540.q: What is the short-term reaction directly after a trauma called, which usually fades within hours to days?
125540.e: The acute stress reaction is a normal, temporary reaction to an extreme event. If the symptoms last a long time, PTSD can develop.
125540.m: An acute stress reaction usually fades quickly.

125541.q: Which diagnosis was newly introduced in ICD-11 for the effects of long-lasting, repeated trauma?
125541.e: Complex PTSD includes the PTSD symptoms plus problems with regulating emotions, self-image and relationships. It occurs, for example, after long captivity or war.

125542.q: What is a stimulus called that triggers memories of the trauma in people with PTSD?
125542.e: A trigger can be a sound, a smell or a place that reminds the person of the trauma. Many of those affected try to avoid such stimuli.
125542.m: A trigger sets off memories of a trauma.

125543.q: Which three core symptoms characterise ADHD?
a: Sadness, lack of drive, sleep disorder
125543.e: ADHD stands for attention deficit hyperactivity disorder. Typical are problems with attention, a strong urge to move and acting impulsively.
125543.m: ADHD shows itself through inattention, hyperactivity and impulsivity.

125544.q: Which active substance is often used to treat ADHD with medication?
125544.e: Methylphenidate is a stimulant that strengthens the effect of messenger substances in the brain. In many people affected it improves attention and self-control.
125544.m: Methylphenidate is a common ADHD medicine.

125545.q: In which Swiss city was methylphenidate first produced by the chemical company Ciba?
125545.e: The chemist Leandro Panizzon produced the substance at Ciba in Basel. Basel is still a centre of the pharmaceutical industry today.

125546.q: What is the form of ADHD without marked hyperactivity often called in everyday language?
125546.e: In the mainly inattentive type, the strong urge to move is missing. Those affected seem more dreamy and distracted.
125546.m: ADD is a form of ADHD without strong hyperactivity.

125547.q: At what stage of life does ADHD begin?
125547.e: ADHD is a developmental disorder. The first signs appear in childhood, even if the diagnosis is sometimes only made later.

125548.q: According to current knowledge, which factor has the greatest influence on the development of ADHD?
125548.e: Twin and family studies show that ADHD is highly heritable. Environmental factors can play a part, but sugar or upbringing alone do not cause ADHD.

125549.q: Which messenger substances are particularly in the focus of ADHD research?
125549.e: In ADHD, signal transmission with dopamine and noradrenaline is altered. These messenger substances are important for attention, motivation and self-control.
125549.m: Dopamine and noradrenaline play an important role in ADHD.

125550.q: What is true of ADHD in adulthood?
125550.e: In many people affected, symptoms remain into adulthood, often in a changed form. Hyperactivity then often becomes inner restlessness.

125551.q: Which character from Heinrich Hoffmann's “Struwwelpeter” is often seen as an early portrayal of ADHD-like behaviour?
a: Augustus who would not eat his soup
125551.e: Fidgety Philip cannot sit still at the table and finally pulls the tablecloth down. That is why people sometimes speak of “Fidgety Philip syndrome”.
125551.m: Fidgety Philip is seen as an early portrayal of hyperactivity.

125552.q: In which two areas do the core features of an autism spectrum disorder show themselves?
125552.e: Autistic people often have difficulties with social interaction and communication. In addition, there are restricted interests and repeated behaviours.
125552.m: Autism affects social communication and repeated patterns of behaviour.

125553.q: Which former diagnosis was merged into autism spectrum disorder in DSM-5?
125553.e: Asperger's syndrome is named after the Austrian paediatrician Hans Asperger. Today the different forms are grouped together as a spectrum.
125553.m: Asperger's syndrome is now part of the autism spectrum.

125554.q: Which child psychiatrist described early childhood autism in the 1940s?
125554.e: In the USA, Leo Kanner published a well-known description of children with autistic features. Early childhood autism is therefore also called Kanner's syndrome.
125554.m: Leo Kanner described early childhood autism.

125555.q: Which Swiss psychiatrist introduced the term “autism” into technical language?
125555.e: Eugen Bleuler was a professor of psychiatry in Zurich and used the word in 1911. He originally meant a withdrawal into one's own inner world.
125555.m: Eugen Bleuler coined the word autism.

125556.q: What does research show about the claimed link between vaccinations and autism?
125556.e: Large studies with millions of children found no link. The study that spread this claim was withdrawn because of falsified data.

125557.q: Why do people speak of a “spectrum” today?
a: The characteristics and the need for support vary greatly
There are exactly three fixed types
125557.e: Autistic people differ greatly in language, abilities and need for support. The term spectrum reflects this variety.
125557.m: Autism shows itself in very different ways.

125558.q: What is self-stimulating, repeated behaviour such as rocking or hand-flapping called?
125558.e: Stimming helps many autistic people to calm down or process stimuli. It is usually harmless and should not simply be suppressed.
125558.m: Stimming helps autistic people regulate themselves.

125559.q: Which special feature of perception is common in autism?
a: Over- or under-sensitivity to sensory stimuli
125559.e: Many autistic people experience sounds, light or touch as very intense or hardly noticeable. Loud, crowded rooms can therefore be very stressful.
125559.m: Autistic people often perceive sensory stimuli differently.

125560.q: Which term describes the view that neurological differences such as autism are natural variations of human beings?
125560.e: The term neurodiversity emphasises the variety of human brains. It aims to make strengths visible and reduce exclusion.
125560.m: Neurodiversity emphasises the variety of human brains.

125561.e: The Viennese doctor Sigmund Freud developed psychoanalysis around 1900. It stresses the importance of unconscious processes.

125562.e: Carl Rogers put the person and their ability to grow at the centre. The therapist accompanies rather than prescribing solutions.

125563.q: According to Carl Rogers, which basic attitude is one of the core conditions of helpful therapy?
a: Rewards in the form of presents
125563.e: Rogers names empathy, unconditional positive regard and genuineness. These attitudes are meant to make change possible for the client.
125563.m: Empathy is a core attitude of client-centred therapy.

125564.q: What is especially at the centre of systemic therapy?
125564.e: Systemic therapy looks at problems in connection with family, partnerships or other groups. Relatives are often included in the therapy.
125564.m: Systemic therapy looks at people within their environment.

125565.q: Which Swiss psychiatrist founded analytical psychology?
125565.e: C. G. Jung worked in Zurich and coined terms such as “collective unconscious” and “archetype”. He later broke away from Freud.
125565.m: C. G. Jung founded analytical psychology.

125566.q: What changed in Switzerland with the prescription model in 2022?
a: Psychological psychotherapy is paid for by basic health insurance when prescribed by a doctor
Only doctors may hold therapy sessions
Therapy is now only available online
125566.e: Before, psychological psychotherapists had to work under a doctor's supervision for the health insurance to pay. Now, on a doctor's prescription, they can bill basic insurance independently.
125566.m: Since the prescription model, basic insurance pays for psychological psychotherapy prescribed by a doctor.

125567.q: Which factor does research consider one of the most important active factors in any psychotherapy?
a: The size of the therapy room
The length of the journey there
125567.e: A trusting relationship between client and therapist helps success across different schools of therapy. This is also called the therapeutic alliance.
125567.m: A good therapeutic relationship is central to the success of therapy.

a: Feelings from earlier relationships are directed at the therapist
Passing files on to the health insurer
125568.e: In transference, the patient unconsciously experiences the therapist in a similar way to important people from the past. These feelings are worked through in therapy.
125568.m: In transference, old relationship patterns appear in therapy.

125569.q: What distinguishes a psychiatrist from a psychologist?
a: A psychiatrist is a doctor and may prescribe medicines
A psychiatrist only works with children
A psychiatrist may not hold conversations
125569.e: Psychiatrists have studied medicine and completed specialist training. Psychologists have studied psychology and do not prescribe medicines.
125569.m: Psychiatrists are doctors and may prescribe medicines.

125570.q: What is the long-established psychiatric university hospital in Zurich called?
125570.e: The Burghölzli opened in 1870 and is now part of the Psychiatric University Hospital Zurich. In the early 20th century it was a world-famous centre of psychiatry.
125570.m: The Burghölzli is the well-known psychiatric hospital in Zurich.

125571.e: Eugen Bleuler introduced the term at the beginning of the 20th century. The word means roughly “split mind”, but it does not mean a split personality.
125571.m: Eugen Bleuler coined the term schizophrenia.

125572.q: Which group of medicines is mainly used to treat psychoses?
125572.e: Antipsychotics, also called neuroleptics, reduce symptoms such as delusions and hallucinations. They act mainly on the dopamine system.

125573.q: Under Swiss law, what is it called when a person is placed in an institution against their will for their own protection?
125573.e: Placement for care and assistance is regulated in the Civil Code. It is only allowed if the necessary treatment or care cannot be provided in any other way.
125573.m: Placement for care and assistance is a protective measure in the Civil Code.

a: A perception without an external stimulus
125574.e: In a hallucination, someone hears, sees or feels something that is not there. Voices that other people cannot hear are common, for example.
125574.m: A hallucination is a perception without a real stimulus.

125575.q: Which substance has long been used as a mood stabiliser in bipolar disorder?
125575.e: Lithium salts can reduce relapses into mania and depression. Because the effective dose is close to the toxic one, the blood level is checked regularly.
125575.m: Lithium stabilises mood in bipolar disorder.

125576.q: What does a psychiatric day clinic offer?
a: Treatment during the day, nights at home
125576.e: The day clinic is a partly inpatient service. Patients spend the day at the clinic with therapies and return home in the evening.
125576.m: In a day clinic you are treated during the day and sleep at home.

a: People are looked down on and excluded because of a characteristic
People are given an award for an achievement
People receive a new identity card
125577.e: In stigmatisation, a characteristic, such as an illness, is linked with negative prejudices. As a result, those affected are put at a disadvantage.
125577.m: Stigmatisation means looking down on people because of a characteristic.

125578.q: What did the Greek word “stigma” originally mean?
a: A prick or a brand mark
125578.e: In ancient Greece, a stigma was a mark that had been burnt or cut into the skin. Today it means a characteristic for which someone is looked down on.
125578.m: A stigma was originally a brand mark.

a: Those affected turn prejudices against themselves
You register yourself with the doctor
125579.e: People who take society's prejudices to heart often feel ashamed and less valuable. This can make recovery even harder.
125579.m: In self-stigmatisation, those affected turn prejudices against themselves.

125580.q: What is a common consequence of the stigmatisation of mental illness?
a: Those affected seek help later or not at all
125580.e: Out of shame and fear of rejection, many people keep their symptoms to themselves. As a result, treatment often starts late.
125580.m: Stigma stops people from seeking help.

125581.q: According to research, which measure is particularly effective in reducing prejudice against people with mental illness?
125581.e: According to the contact hypothesis, direct encounters reduce prejudice. That is why personal accounts from those affected are often used in anti-stigma programmes.

125582.q: Which wording is considered more respectful?
125582.e: This wording puts the person before the illness. That way the person is not reduced to their diagnosis.
125582.m: Respectful language puts the person before the diagnosis.

125583.q: What is the Swiss campaign called that encourages people to talk openly about mental health?
125583.e: The campaign is a project of the German-speaking cantons and the Pro Mente Sana foundation on behalf of Health Promotion Switzerland. It gives tips on how to start conversations about mental health problems.
125583.m: The campaign “Wie geht's dir?” encourages conversations about mental health.

125584.q: What is meant by structural discrimination against people with mental illness?
a: Disadvantage caused by rules and institutions
125584.e: Structural discrimination comes from laws, procedures or the way resources are shared out, not from individual prejudices. One example is poorer care compared with physical illnesses.
125584.m: Structural discrimination is built into rules and institutions.

125585.q: What can children and young people contact the Pro Juventute 147 helpline about?
125585.e: The 147 helpline is open for any topic, such as stress, bullying, family or worries about the future. No worry is too small.
125585.m: You can talk about any worry on 147.

125586.q: When can you reach the 147 helpline?
125586.e: The 147 helpline can be reached around the clock, 365 days a year. That way, young people can find support at night too.
125586.m: The 147 helpline is available day and night.

125587.q: How much does a call to the 147 helpline cost?
a: A flat rate of ten francs
It varies from canton to canton
125587.e: The helpline is free for children and young people. That way no one has to go without help for lack of money.

125588.q: Apart from by phone, how else can you reach the 147 helpline?
a: By text message, chat and email
Only in person at a counter
125588.e: Besides the phone, advice is available by text message, in a chat and by email. Many young people prefer writing to calling.
125588.m: The 147 helpline can also be reached by text, chat and email.

125589.q: What is true of conversations with the 147 helpline?
125589.e: The advice is confidential, and you do not have to give your name. This makes it easier to talk about difficult topics too.
125589.m: On 147 you can talk about your worries in confidence.

125590.q: What kind of organisation is Pro Juventute?
a: A Swiss foundation for children and young people
125590.e: Pro Juventute is a non-profit foundation. It supports children, young people and parents with advice and projects.
125590.m: Pro Juventute is a foundation for children and young people.

125591.q: What is the phone number of Die Dargebotene Hand, the Swiss helpline for adults?
125591.e: Die Dargebotene Hand can be reached on 143 and is mainly for adults. The number 145 belongs to Tox Info, 118 to the fire brigade.
125591.m: Die Dargebotene Hand has the number 143.

125592.q: Which number do you dial in Switzerland for the ambulance service when a life is in acute danger?
125592.e: In a medical emergency such as an acute danger to life, you call the ambulance service on 144. The 147 helpline is for talking about worries, and 145 is the number of Tox Info.
125592.m: When a life is in acute danger, you dial 144.

125593.q: Which American psychiatrist is regarded as the founder of cognitive therapy?
125593.e: Aaron T. Beck first developed cognitive therapy for depression. He showed how negative thought patterns influence feelings.
125593.m: Aaron T. Beck founded cognitive therapy.

125594.q: Who developed rational emotive behaviour therapy?
125594.e: Albert Ellis believed that irrational beliefs cause distressing feelings. His method is one of the roots of cognitive behavioural therapy.
125594.m: Albert Ellis developed rational emotive behaviour therapy.

125595.q: What does Beck's cognitive triad refer to?
a: A negative view of yourself, the world and the future
125595.e: Beck described a negative view of oneself, one's surroundings and the future in depression. The therapy examines these thoughts together.
125595.m: The cognitive triad is a negative view of yourself, the world and the future.

125596.q: What is the thinking error called in which you conclude the worst possible outcome from a small problem?
125596.e: In catastrophising, one mistake immediately becomes total failure. Therapy helps to find more realistic thoughts.
125596.m: Catastrophising turns small things into disasters.

125597.q: What does the “B” stand for in Albert Ellis's ABC model?
125597.e: A is the activating event, B the belief and C the consequence. It is not the event alone but how it is judged that determines the feeling.
125597.m: In the ABC model, how an event is judged determines the feeling.

125598.q: What is the technique called in which unhelpful thoughts are recognised, checked and replaced with more helpful ones?
125598.e: In cognitive restructuring, you look for evidence for and against a thought. This leads to more balanced views.

125599.q: What is the aim of behavioural activation in depression?
a: Staying in bed as much as possible
125599.e: Depressed people often withdraw, which lowers their mood further. Planned, positive activities break this cycle.
125599.m: Behavioural activation gets mood going again through activity.

125600.q: What is the thinking error called in which only extremes such as “perfect” or “total failure” are seen?
125600.e: In black-and-white thinking, there are no shades in between. Anyone who is not perfect then sees themselves straight away as a failure.
125600.m: Black-and-white thinking has no shades in between.

125601.q: Which skill do people practise in many modern behavioural therapies by perceiving the moment consciously and without judging it?
125601.e: Mindfulness is a core element of newer methods such as Marsha Linehan's dialectical behaviour therapy. You learn to notice thoughts and feelings without reacting to them straight away.
125601.m: Mindfulness means experiencing the moment consciously and without judging.

a: The interaction between mind and body
125602.e: The term is made up of the Greek “psyche” (soul) and “soma” (body). Psychosomatics studies how mental factors influence physical complaints and the other way round.
125602.m: Psychosomatics studies the interplay between mind and body.

125603.q: Which model explains illness as the interplay of biological, psychological and social factors?
125603.e: The biopsychosocial model was made known by the psychiatrist George Engel. It adds the mind and the environment to the purely biological view.
125603.m: The biopsychosocial model connects body, mind and social environment.

125604.q: Which hormone does the adrenal cortex release in larger amounts during lasting stress?
125604.e: Cortisol provides energy and helps to cope with strain. If it stays high for a long time, it can weaken the immune system and disturb sleep.
125604.m: Cortisol is an important stress hormone.

a: Physical complaints without a sufficient physical cause being found
A broken bone after a fall
A heart disease present from birth
125605.e: Those affected really suffer from pain or other complaints, but the examinations do not explain them sufficiently. The complaints are not imagined.
125605.m: In somatoform disorders, real complaints have no sufficient physical cause.

125606.q: Which complaint is particularly often partly caused by stress and tension?
125606.e: Under stress, the neck and head muscles tense up. This can trigger a pressing headache.

125607.q: What is the effect called that arises solely from positive expectations of a treatment?
125607.e: Just expecting a remedy to help can measurably relieve complaints. Placebo means “I shall please” in Latin.
125607.m: The placebo effect comes from positive expectations.

125608.q: What is the effect called in which negative expectations cause or worsen complaints?
125608.e: People who expect side effects, for example, feel them more often, even with a dummy pill. Nocebo means “I shall harm” in Latin.
125608.m: Negative expectations can trigger complaints through the nocebo effect.

125609.q: Which researcher shaped the modern concept of stress with the “general adaptation syndrome”?
125609.e: Hans Selye described how the body reacts to lasting strain in phases: alarm, resistance and exhaustion. He made the term stress known in medicine.
125609.m: Hans Selye shaped the modern understanding of stress.

125610.q: Which two postulates form the basis of the special theory of relativity?
a: The principle of relativity and the constancy of the speed of light
Conservation of energy and conservation of momentum
The principle of inertia and the law of gravitation
The uncertainty principle and wave-particle duality
125610.e: First, the laws of nature are the same in all inertial frames. Second, the speed of light in a vacuum is the same for all observers, regardless of how the source moves.
125610.m: Special relativity is based on the principle of relativity and the constant speed of light.

125611.q: What is the region of spacetime called that a signal from an event can reach at most at the speed of light?
125611.e: In a spacetime diagram, the paths of light rays form a cone around the event. Only events inside this cone can be causally connected.
125611.m: The light cone limits what an event can influence.

a: A frame of reference without acceleration
A braking car as a frame of reference
125612.e: In an inertial frame, a body on which no forces act moves in a straight line at constant speed. The frame is at rest or moves at constant velocity.
125612.m: An inertial frame is a non-accelerating frame of reference.

125613.q: A spaceship flies at 0.5 c and launches a probe forwards at 0.5 c relative to the ship. How fast is the probe relative to the starting point?
125613.e: According to relativistic velocity addition, u = (v + w) / (1 + vw/c²). So (0.5 + 0.5) / (1 + 0.25) = 1 / 1.25 = 0.8 c.
125613.m: Velocities added relativistically never exceed the speed of light.

125614.q: Which mathematician combined space and time into a four-dimensional spacetime?
125614.e: Hermann Minkowski, a former teacher of Einstein’s at ETH Zurich, formulated the theory geometrically. Space and time form a single spacetime.
125614.m: Hermann Minkowski shaped the concept of spacetime.

125615.q: How large is the relativistic kinetic energy of a body with mass m at 0.6 c (γ = 1.25)?
125615.e: Relativistically, E_kin = (γ minus 1)mc² = (1.25 minus 1)mc² = 0.25 mc². The classical formula ½mv² would give only 0.18 mc² and is too inaccurate at this speed.
125615.m: Relativistically, kinetic energy is the total energy minus the rest energy.

125616.q: According to special relativity, which relation between energy E and momentum p applies to a photon?
125616.e: In general, E² = (pc)² + (mc²)². Because a photon has no rest mass, E = pc remains.
125616.m: For massless particles, energy equals momentum times the speed of light.

125617.q: What do you observe in the light from a source moving away from us at high speed?
a: It is shifted to longer wavelengths
It is shifted to shorter wavelengths
125617.e: In the relativistic Doppler effect, the light from a receding source is redshifted. Unlike with sound, time dilation also plays a part.
125617.m: Light from a receding source is redshifted.

125618.q: Which thought experiment, according to Einstein himself, already occupied him as a teenager?
a: Riding along behind a beam of light
Shutting a cat in a box
125618.e: Einstein wondered what a light wave would look like if you ran alongside it. This idea later led him to realise that light travels at the same speed for every observer.
125618.m: Einstein imagined following a beam of light at an early age.

125619.q: What was the Michelson-Morley experiment originally meant to detect?
a: The Earth’s motion through the ether
125619.e: People believed that light travelled in a medium at rest, the ether. The Earth’s motion was supposed to produce a measurable “ether wind”.
125619.m: The experiment looked for the ether wind.

125620.q: Which measuring instrument did Michelson and Morley use?
125620.e: The Michelson interferometer splits a beam of light into two perpendicular beams and brings them back together. Even the tiniest differences in travel time become visible.
125620.m: Michelson and Morley measured with an interferometer.

125621.q: Which motion of the Earth was supposed to cause a measurable effect in the experiment?
a: Its orbit around the Sun at about 30 km/s
The Moon’s motion around the Earth
The plate tectonics of the continents
125621.e: The Earth orbits the Sun at about 30 kilometres per second. Relative to an ether at rest, this should have given a clear difference in travel time.
125621.m: The Earth moves around the Sun at about 30 km/s.

125622.q: Which observation in the interferometer would have pointed to an ether wind?
a: A shift of the interference fringes when the apparatus was turned
A change in the colour of the light
125622.e: When the apparatus was turned, the travel times in the two arms should have changed. That would have shifted the light and dark fringes.
125622.m: An ether wind would have shifted the interference fringes.

125623.q: What was the apparatus mounted on so that it could be turned with little vibration?
a: On a stone slab floating in mercury
On a wooden table with wheels
125623.e: The heavy stone slab floated in a basin of mercury. This allowed it to be turned smoothly without vibrations disturbing the measurement.

125624.q: What result did the Michelson-Morley experiment produce?
a: The ether wind was exactly as large as expected
The ether wind was twice as large as expected
The light was stopped in the interferometer
125624.e: The interference fringes hardly moved when the apparatus was turned. This null result was a big surprise, as a clear effect had been expected.
125624.m: The Michelson-Morley experiment found no ether wind.

125625.q: Which statement about light follows from the result of the Michelson-Morley experiment?
a: The speed of light is the same in all directions
Light is faster in the direction of the Earth’s motion
Light is slowed down by the ether
Light only travels in a vacuum
125625.e: However the apparatus was turned, the light took the same time in both arms. In 1905, Einstein made the constancy of the speed of light a cornerstone of special relativity.
125625.m: The speed of light does not depend on the Earth’s motion.

125626.q: How did Michelson and Morley lengthen the light path in their interferometer to increase its sensitivity?
a: By reflecting it several times off mirrors
With a tunnel in a mountain
125626.e: The light was sent back and forth between mirrors several times. A longer light path makes small differences in travel time easier to measure.
125626.m: Multiple reflections lengthened the light path in the experiment.

125627.q: What does time dilation in special relativity state?
a: All clocks run at the same rate
125627.e: For an observer, less time passes on a clock moving relative to them. The effect only becomes clear at very high speeds.
125627.m: For an observer at rest, moving clocks run slow.

125628.q: With what did researchers demonstrate time dilation on passenger aircraft in 1971?
125628.e: Joseph Hafele and Richard Keating flew atomic clocks around the Earth and compared them with clocks on the ground. The tiny differences agreed with the theory of relativity.
125628.m: Atomic clocks on aircraft confirmed time dilation.

125629.q: What is the time shown by a clock moving along with an object, in its own rest frame, called?
125629.e: Proper time is the time measured by a clock moving with the object. It is the same in every frame of reference and is therefore especially important.
125629.m: Proper time is the time in a clock’s rest frame.

125630.q: Roughly how large is the Lorentz factor γ at a speed of 0.99 c?
125630.e: γ = 1 / √(1 minus 0.99²) = 1 / √0.0199 ≈ 1 / 0.141 ≈ 7.1. Clocks then run about seven times slower.
125630.m: Close to the speed of light, the Lorentz factor becomes very large.

125631.q: Which thought experiment is often used to derive time dilation?
125631.e: In the light clock, a pulse of light travels back and forth between two mirrors. For an outside observer, the light in the moving clock travels a longer path, so the clock ticks more slowly.
125631.m: The light clock illustrates time dilation.

125632.q: Two spaceships pass each other at constant velocity. What do the crews notice about each other’s clock?
a: Both see the other clock running slow
Only one crew sees an effect
Both see the other clock running fast
Both clocks run at the same rate
125632.e: Between two inertial frames, time dilation is symmetrical. Each side may regard itself as at rest and measures the other’s clock as running slow.
125632.m: Between inertial frames, time dilation is mutual.

125633.q: Which relation describes time dilation if Δt₀ is the proper time?
125633.e: Because γ is always at least 1, the time Δt measured in the frame at rest is greater than the proper time. So the moving clock shows less time.
125633.m: The observed time is longer than the proper time by the factor γ.

125634.q: From what speed does time dilation occur?
a: At any speed, but it is tiny in everyday life
Only from half the speed of light
Only at exactly the speed of light
Only from the speed of sound
125634.e: The Lorentz factor is greater than 1 at any speed, but only very slightly at everyday speeds. With modern atomic clocks, the effect can even be detected at cycling speed.
125634.m: Time dilation exists at any speed; in everyday life it is just tiny.

a: Moving bodies are shortened in the direction of motion
125635.e: An observer measures a body moving relative to them as shorter in the direction of motion than at rest. Nothing changes at right angles to the motion.
125635.m: Moving bodies appear shortened in the direction of motion.

125636.q: In which direction does length contraction occur?
a: Only in the direction of motion
Only at right angles to the motion
125636.e: The Lorentz transformation only changes the coordinate in the direction of motion. The dimensions at right angles to it stay the same.
125636.m: Length contraction only acts in the direction of motion.

125637.q: A spaceship is 100 m long at rest. What length does an observer measure as it flies past at 0.6 c?
125637.m: The moving length is shorter than the proper length by the Lorentz factor.
