126894.q: A quadrat measures 50 cm by 50 cm and contains 3 plants on average. What is the density per m²?
126894.e: The quadrat has an area of 0.25 m². One square metre holds four such areas, so 3 times 4 = 12 plants.
126894.m: With small quadrats, you have to convert the area into square metres.

126895.q: A species occurs in 14 out of 20 quadrats. What is its frequency?
126895.e: Frequency is the share of quadrats containing the species. 14 divided by 20 gives 0.7, so 70%.
126895.m: Frequency shows in how many sample plots a species occurs.

126896.q: Why are quadrats for repeat surveys often marked permanently in the field?
a: To follow changes in exactly the same place over years
To protect the plants inside them
To make the area bigger every year
126896.e: Such permanent quadrats are marked, for example, with metal markers in the ground. Because the same area is always surveyed, differences show real changes in the vegetation.
126896.m: Permanent quadrats make changes in the same place visible over years.

126897.q: For which organisms is the quadrat method especially well suited?
a: For organisms that are fixed in place or slow
126897.e: Plants, lichens or barnacles stay in place while you count. Mobile animals would escape from the frame or be counted twice.
126897.m: The quadrat method suits living things that hardly move.

126898.q: Which rule often applies to plants growing exactly on the edge of a quadrat?
a: You only count them on two set sides
You leave them out on all sides
126898.e: With a fixed edge rule, edge plants are not systematically counted too often or too rarely. It is important that everyone involved uses the same rule.
126898.m: A fixed edge rule prevents counting errors at the edge of the quadrat.

126899.q: How do you choose the position of quadrats properly at random?
a: With random numbers as coordinates in a grid
By throwing the frame over your shoulder
Where most of the flowers are
126899.e: Random numbers for x and y fix the position objectively. Throwing the frame blindly seems random but is often biased.
126899.m: Random coordinates are more objective than a thrown frame.

126900.q: Which measure do you get when you divide the number of individuals of a species counted by the area studied?
126900.e: The density of individuals shows how many individuals occur per unit of area, for example 5 per m². It is a measure of the abundance of a species.
126900.m: Density is the number of individuals per area.

126901.q: What is a transect in field ecology?
a: A line or strip along which you record species
A measuring tower in the forest
126901.e: For a transect, you lay a line through a habitat and record the species along this line. This lets you see changes across space.
126901.m: A transect is a survey line through a habitat.

126902.q: What are transects especially suitable for?
a: For changes along an environmental gradient
For counting animals in the lab
For finding out the age of a tree
126902.e: A transect from the lakeshore inland or from forest into meadow shows how species change with moisture or light. Such transitions are called gradients.
126902.m: Transects show how species change along a gradient.

126903.q: How does a belt transect differ from a line transect?
a: It is a strip of a certain width
It is only walked at night
It always runs in a circle
126903.e: In a line transect, you only count what touches the line. In a belt transect, you study a strip, often made of quadrats placed in a row.
126903.m: A belt transect is a wide survey strip instead of a thin line.

126904.q: How are butterflies often recorded in monitoring programmes?
a: On fixed routes in suitable weather
With pitfall traps in the leaf litter
126904.e: On butterfly transects, you walk a fixed route at a steady pace and note the butterflies in a certain zone. This is only done in sunshine, warmth and light wind.
126904.m: Butterflies are often counted on fixed routes in good weather.

126905.q: Why are animals far away noted less often in counts along a transect?
a: They are smaller than nearby animals
They do not count as part of the habitat
They always run towards the line
126905.e: Animals far away are spotted less often than nearby ones. In distance sampling, the distances are therefore measured and used to estimate how many animals were missed.
126905.m: The further away an animal is, the more likely it is to be missed.

126906.q: Why are transects in the Alps often laid from the valley up to the summit region?
a: To study how species change with altitude
Because hiking paths only run that way
To measure the steepness of the slope
Because more species live higher up
126906.e: With altitude, temperature and the length of the growing season decrease. Altitude transects show how species shift, for example as a result of climate change.
126906.m: Altitude transects show how species change with height.

126907.q: How does the line-point method along a transect work?
a: At fixed intervals, you note the plant that is touched
You count all animals in a circle
You measure the length of every plant
You photograph the line from the air
126907.e: At each set point, for example every 10 cm, you record which plant touches the line there. From this you can calculate the share of each species.
126907.m: In the line-point method, you record plants at fixed points along a line.

126908.q: Which Swiss programme has been recording butterflies and breeding birds, among others, on fixed routes in one-kilometre squares since the early 2000s?
126908.e: Biodiversity Monitoring Switzerland is run on behalf of the Federal Office for the Environment. It observes species diversity on evenly spread sample areas.
126908.m: Biodiversity Monitoring Switzerland tracks species diversity over many years.

126909.q: You catch and mark 40 lizards. Later you catch 50, of which 10 are marked. What is the estimated population according to Lincoln-Petersen?
126909.e: The formula is N = M times C divided by R. So 40 times 50 divided by 10 = 200 animals.
126909.m: The share of marked animals in the second catch reveals the size of the population.

126910.q: In the first catch, 60 beetles are marked. In the second catch, 12 of 80 beetles are marked. What is the estimate?
126910.e: N = 60 times 80 divided by 12 = 4,800 divided by 12 = 400. To check: 12 out of 80 is 15%, and 60 out of 400 is also 15%.
126910.m: With Lincoln-Petersen, the share of marked animals is the same in the catch and the population.

126911.q: Which assumption is the simple capture-recapture method based on?
a: The population is closed between the catches
All the animals are the same age
126911.e: Between the catches there should be no births, deaths, arrivals or departures. Otherwise the ratio of marked animals is no longer right.
126911.m: The simple method assumes a closed population.

126912.q: What happens to the estimate if many animals lose their markings?
126912.e: Lost markings lower the number of marked animals recaptured, R. Since R is in the denominator, N becomes too large.
126912.m: Lost markings lead to too high a population estimate.

126913.q: Marked animals like to go back to the trap because there was food in it. What effect does this have?
126913.e: Trap-happy animals increase the share of marked animals in the second catch. A large R in the denominator gives too small an estimate.
126913.m: Trap-happy animals make the estimated population smaller.

126914.q: Which requirement must a marking meet in the capture-recapture method?
a: It must not affect the animal’s survival
It must be easy for predators to see
It must disappear after one day
It must stop the animal from moving around
126914.e: A bright colour could make marked animals easier for enemies to see. Then they die more often, and the estimate is wrong.
126914.m: A good marking does not harm the animal or change its behaviour.

126915.q: Which Swiss institution coordinates the scientific ringing of birds?
a: The Swiss Ornithological Institute in Sempach
The Swiss Federal Research Institute WSL
The Natural History Museum of Bern
126915.e: The Swiss Ornithological Institute in Sempach runs Switzerland’s ringing centre. Recoveries of ringed birds provide data on migration routes, age and numbers.
126915.m: The Swiss Ornithological Institute in Sempach coordinates bird ringing in Switzerland.

126916.q: Why are tiny chips often placed under the skin of fish or amphibians instead of colour markings?
a: This way each animal can be recognised individually and permanently
This makes the animals grow faster
This makes the animals easier for predators to see
126916.e: A chip without its own battery is read with a scanner and has a unique number. Colour, on the other hand, can wash off or attract predators.
126916.m: A chip under the skin makes animals individually recognisable.

126917.q: Why does the capture-recapture estimate become inaccurate if there are only very few marked animals in the second catch?
a: Even one animal more or less changes the result a lot
Because then all the animals are marked
Because the formula only works for birds
Because then no animals live in the area any more
126917.e: The number of marked animals recaptured is in the denominator. If it is very small, chance changes the result a lot. Larger samples give more reliable estimates.
126917.m: Few recaptures make the estimate unreliable.

126918.q: What is meant by remote sensing?
a: Collecting data without direct contact, for example by satellite
126918.e: Remote sensing measures the radiation given off or reflected by the Earth’s surface. Satellites, aircraft or drones are used as platforms.
126918.m: Remote sensing records the Earth’s surface from a distance.

126919.q: Which method sends out laser pulses itself and can therefore measure the height of trees?
126919.e: LiDAR measures how long laser pulses take to reach the ground and the tree crown. This produces a three-dimensional picture of the forest.
126919.m: LiDAR uses laser pulses to measure the three-dimensional structure of vegetation.

126920.q: What advantage does radar have over optical satellite images?
a: It also works through clouds and at night
126920.e: Radar sends out microwaves, which largely pass through clouds. Because it uses its own radiation, it needs no sunlight.
126920.m: Radar provides images regardless of clouds and daylight.

126921.q: What does the spatial resolution of a satellite image describe?
a: The size of one pixel on the ground
The number of images per year
126921.e: At a resolution of 10 m, one pixel covers 10 by 10 m. Smaller objects such as individual shrubs cannot be seen.
126921.m: Spatial resolution tells you how large one pixel is on the ground.

126922.q: Which European Earth observation programme do the Sentinel satellites belong to?
126922.e: Copernicus is the EU’s Earth observation programme. Its Sentinel satellites provide freely available data, for example on vegetation, oceans and the atmosphere.
126922.m: The Sentinel satellites belong to the Copernicus programme.

126923.q: Which US satellite series has been delivering continuous images of the land surface since the 1970s?
126923.e: Landsat is the longest continuous image series of the land surface from space. It lets scientists follow changes in forests and glaciers over decades.
126923.m: Landsat shows changes to the Earth’s surface over decades.

126924.q: What advantage do drones have over satellites when mapping small areas?
126924.e: Drones fly low and reach resolutions of a few centimetres. However, they are only suitable for small areas.
126924.m: Drones provide very detailed images of small areas.

126925.q: Why is field data, known as ground truth, still needed despite satellite images?
a: To check and calibrate the analysis
126925.e: Only with comparison data from the ground do you know which image value belongs to which habitat. It is also used to check how accurate a map is.
126925.m: Field data checks whether the analysis of satellite images is correct.

126926.q: What distinguishes a hyperspectral sensor from a multispectral sensor?
a: It measures a great many narrow wavelength ranges
It has its own light source
It only takes black and white images
126926.e: Multispectral sensors record a few broad channels. Hyperspectral sensors measure hundreds of narrow channels and can therefore detect fine differences, for example between plant species.
126926.m: Hyperspectral sensors split light into a great many narrow channels.

126927.q: How is the vegetation index NDVI calculated?
a: (NIR minus red) divided by (NIR plus red)
126927.e: The NDVI compares near infrared (NIR) with red light. Normalising by the sum makes images taken in different lighting easier to compare.
126927.m: The NDVI compares near infrared with red light.

126928.q: Why do healthy leaves reflect near infrared particularly strongly?
a: Because of the cell structure inside the leaf
Because of the wax layer alone
Because of the water in the roots
126928.e: The loose tissue inside the leaf scatters near infrared many times and throws much of it back. In damaged leaves, this reflection decreases.
126928.m: Leaf tissue scatters near infrared strongly back.

126929.q: Why does green vegetation reflect little red light?
a: Red light passes into the soil
Red turns into heat in the trunk
126929.e: Chlorophyll uses red and blue light for photosynthesis. That is why only a little red is reflected.
126929.m: Chlorophyll absorbs red light for photosynthesis.

126930.q: In which range of values does the NDVI lie?
126930.e: Because the difference and the sum of the same values are divided, the result can never be larger than 1 in size. Dense green vegetation reaches values of around 0.8 to 0.9.
126930.m: The NDVI always lies between minus one and plus one.

126931.q: A pixel has a reflectance of 0.5 in the near infrared and 0.1 in the red. What is the NDVI?
126931.e: NDVI = (0.5 minus 0.1) ÷ (0.5 + 0.1) = 0.4 ÷ 0.6, so about 0.67. This points to dense, healthy vegetation.
126931.m: A high NDVI indicates a lot of green vegetation.

126932.q: Which surface typically shows negative NDVI values?
126932.e: Water reflects very little in the near infrared, often less than in the red. This makes the numerator negative.
126932.m: Open water usually has a negative NDVI.

126933.q: What problem does the NDVI have with very dense vegetation?
a: It saturates and barely responds any more
126933.e: Above a certain amount of leaves, the NDVI hardly rises any more, even though more biomass is added. For dense forests, other indices are therefore often used.
126933.m: With very dense vegetation, the NDVI reaches its limit.

126934.q: What are NDVI time series over a year used for?
a: To track leaf-out, growing season and drought stress
To measure the height of mountains
126934.e: When the NDVI rises in spring, vegetation starts to grow. An unusual drop in summer can point to drought.
126934.m: NDVI time series show the vegetation’s yearly cycle.

a: DNA that living things release into their surroundings
126935.e: Living things constantly shed cells, mucus, hair or droppings. This DNA can be obtained from water, soil or air samples.
126935.m: Environmental DNA comes from traces that living things leave behind.

126936.q: What advantage does environmental DNA offer for detecting rare species?
a: You do not have to see or catch the animals
You learn the exact age of every animal
You can use it to tag animals
126936.e: A water sample can show that a shy fish or newt lives in the water. The animals are not disturbed.
126936.m: With environmental DNA, species can be detected without disturbing them.

126937.q: What is meant by eDNA metabarcoding?
a: Identifying many species in a sample at once using short DNA sections
Counting a single species under the microscope
Fully decoding the genome of one species
126937.e: In metabarcoding, a typical DNA section from all organisms in a sample is copied and sequenced. Comparison with databases shows which species it contains.
126937.m: Metabarcoding identifies many species in a single sample.

126938.q: Which method is usually used to detect one specific species with eDNA?
126938.e: Species-specific primers copy only the DNA of the species being looked for. Quantitative PCR shows whether it is present and how much.
126938.m: qPCR looks specifically for the DNA of one particular species.

126939.q: Why does environmental DNA in water usually only show the recent presence of a species?
a: The DNA is broken down quickly by UV light, heat and microbes
The DNA sinks into the ground at once
The DNA evaporates when it rains
126939.e: In water, free DNA often breaks down within days to weeks. A detection therefore usually means that the species was there a short time ago.
126939.m: Environmental DNA breaks down relatively quickly in water.

126940.q: Why do eDNA surveys take blank samples of clean water along?
126940.e: Because even tiny traces of DNA can be detected, equipment or hands can contaminate samples. If the blank sample shows DNA, the measurement is doubtful.
126940.m: Blank samples reveal contamination in eDNA analyses.

126941.q: Why is an eDNA detection in a river imprecise about location?
a: The DNA is carried downstream by the current
Fish leave no DNA in the water
River water destroys all DNA at once
126941.e: A sample can contain DNA from animals living some way upstream. You therefore have to take the direction of flow and breakdown into account.
126941.m: In rivers, environmental DNA can come from further upstream.

126942.q: Why is a good reference database important for eDNA metabarcoding?
a: Only then can the sequences found be assigned to species
It replaces sampling in the field
It counts the individuals of each species
126942.e: A DNA sequence only becomes meaningful when it can be compared with known sequences of particular species. If a species is missing from the database, it remains unrecognised.
126942.m: Without a reference database, eDNA sequences cannot be assigned to a species.

126943.q: What does a species accumulation curve show?
a: The species found in relation to sampling effort
The size of a population over time
The number of individuals per species
126943.e: The x-axis shows the number of samples, the y-axis the cumulative number of species. The curve rises steeply at first and flattens out later.
126943.m: The species accumulation curve shows how more samples add more species.

126944.q: What does it mean when a species accumulation curve clearly flattens out?
a: Most species have probably been recorded
There are no species in the area
126944.e: New samples then bring hardly any new species. In that case the survey is fairly complete.
126944.m: A flat curve shows an almost complete species survey.

126945.q: What follows if the species accumulation curve is still rising steeply at the end?
a: Many species are still missing, more samples are needed
The species diversity is already fully known
The area is poor in species
The curve has been drawn wrongly
126945.e: Every extra sample still brings new species. The observed number of species then clearly underestimates the true number.
126945.m: A steep curve shows that many species are still undiscovered.

126946.q: What is rarefaction used for with species counts?
a: To compare species counts at equal effort
To count rare animals in the zoo
126946.e: More samples almost always produce more species. Rarefaction scales all samples down to the same size so that the comparison is fair.
126946.m: Rarefaction makes species counts comparable when effort differs.

126947.q: You find 30 species, 8 of them with only one individual and 4 with only two. What is the Chao1 estimate (S plus F1² divided by 2 times F2)?
126947.e: F1² is 8 times 8 = 64, and 2 times F2 is 8. So 30 + 64 ÷ 8 = 30 + 8 = 38 species.
126947.m: Many single finds point to species not yet discovered.

126948.q: Which relationship is described by the formula S = c times A to the power of z?
a: The ten per cent rule of energy
126948.e: The formula describes how the number of species S increases with area A. The exponent z is usually well below 1, so the curve becomes flatter.
126948.m: Larger areas contain more species, but not proportionally more.

126949.q: In species estimates, what are singletons?
a: Species found with only one individual
Species that live on only one island
126949.e: Many singletons show that rare species were only just recorded. Estimators such as Chao1 use them to estimate undiscovered species.
126949.m: Singletons are species found only a single time.

126950.q: Why are species accumulation curves averaged over many random orders of samples?
a: Because the shape of the curve depends on the order of the samples
Because otherwise the number of species falls
Because only then is the area known
126950.e: If you happen to start with a species-rich sample, the curve rises more steeply at first. Averaging over many orders produces a smooth, unbiased curve.
126950.m: Averaging over orders smooths the species accumulation curve.

126951.q: What does the cover of a plant species indicate?
a: The share of the area it covers seen vertically from above
126951.e: You imagine the plant parts projected from above and estimate the covered share in per cent. In this way large plants count more than many small ones.
126951.m: Cover measures the area covered from above in per cent.

126952.q: Why can the sum of the cover values of all species be over 100 %?
126952.e: In a forest, trees, shrubs and herbs cover the same patch of ground. Each species is estimated on its own, so the sum can exceed 100 %.
126952.m: Overlapping plant layers can together cover more than 100 %.

126953.q: Which botanist born in Chur gave his name to a widely used scale for cover and abundance?
126953.e: Josias Braun-Blanquet is regarded as the founder of plant sociology. His method of recording vegetation is still used worldwide today.
126953.m: The Braun-Blanquet scale comes from a botanist from the Grisons.

126954.q: In a sample plot of 4 m², a plant species covers about 1 m² seen from above. What is its cover?
126954.e: Cover is the share of the area that is covered. 1 m² out of 4 m² is a quarter, so 25 %.
126954.m: Cover is the covered share of the area in per cent.

126955.q: What is the Braun-Blanquet scale used for in vegetation surveys?
a: To estimate cover and abundance of plant species
To determine the age of trees
126955.e: With the Braun-Blanquet scale you estimate, for each plant species in a plot, how much it covers and how common it is. It ranges from “r” for very rare to 5 for over 75 % cover.
126955.m: The Braun-Blanquet scale estimates cover and abundance of plant species.

126956.q: What is a well-known weakness of estimated cover values?
a: You need a satellite for them
126956.e: Cover values are usually estimated by eye. Experience and how someone feels on the day affect the result, so surveyors are trained and their estimates compared.
126956.m: Estimated cover values also depend on the person estimating.

126957.q: In a point survey with 100 points, a species is hit at 35 points. What is its cover?
126957.e: The share of hits estimates cover directly. 35 out of 100 points gives 35 %.
126957.m: In the point method, the share of hits equals the cover.

126958.q: Which tool can be used to measure canopy closure in a forest objectively?
a: Photos taken upwards through a fisheye lens
126958.e: Hemispherical photos show the whole sky above a point. Software calculates the share covered by tree crowns.
126958.m: Fisheye photos measure how much tree crowns cover the sky.

126959.q: Why does the phenological network observe the same plants at the same site every year if possible?
a: So that differences between years are due to the weather
Because other plants do not flower
So that the plants get used to people
126959.e: Location, soil and genes also affect when plants flower. If these stay the same, the differences between years mainly reflect weather and climate.
126959.m: Fixed observation plants make differences between years comparable.

126960.q: Which federal office runs Switzerland’s nationwide phenological observation network?
126960.e: MeteoSwiss has been collecting observations on leaf-out, flowering and autumn colouring since 1951. The long records show how vegetation responds to the climate.
126960.m: MeteoSwiss runs the phenological observation network.

126961.q: Which tree in Geneva is the official herald of spring, whose first leaf has been recorded since the early 19th century?
126961.e: The leaf-out of the official horse chestnut on the Promenade de la Treille has been noted in Geneva for over 200 years. It is one of the longest phenological records.
126961.m: The Geneva horse chestnut provides a very long phenological record.

126962.q: What trend do long phenological records in Switzerland show for the spring phases?
a: On average they occur earlier today
They no longer happen at all
126962.e: With rising temperatures, leaf-out and flowering now begin earlier on average than a few decades ago. This is a visible sign of climate change.
126962.m: Because of warming, spring begins earlier in nature.

126963.q: Which environmental factor has a particularly strong influence on when many trees come into leaf?
a: The temperature in the weeks before
The amount of snow the previous year
126963.e: Many trees come into leaf when enough warmth has built up in spring. That is why a warm March brings leaf-out forward.
126963.m: Warmth in spring makes trees come into leaf earlier.

126964.q: Who provides most of the observations in Switzerland’s phenological observation network?
126964.e: Many volunteers report over the years when certain plants flower or come into leaf at their site. Their long commitment makes the data records valuable.
126964.m: Volunteers contribute a lot to phenological observations.

126965.q: What is meant by a phenological mismatch?
a: Time-shifted cycles of species that depend on each other
A mistake in the weather forecast
126965.e: If, for example, caterpillars hatch earlier while tits still breed at the usual time, the young birds later lack food. Species react to warming to different degrees.
126965.m: A mismatch occurs when dependent species drift apart in time.

126966.q: Why are phenological data important for allergy information?
a: They show when plants such as birches begin to flower
They measure the amount of fine dust
They count the insects in the air
126966.e: The start of flowering shows when the pollen season begins. People with pollen allergies can then prepare in good time.
126966.m: Phenological data help to estimate when the pollen season begins.

a: The diameter or circumference of a tree trunk
126967.e: Dendrometers record how a trunk grows or shrinks. Some measure only occasionally, others record continuously.
126967.m: A dendrometer measures the thickness of a tree trunk.

a: A band with a scale fastened around the trunk
A drill for taking wood samples
A laser for measuring tree height
126968.e: The band stays permanently around the trunk. As the tree grows, the scale shifts and you read off the increase in circumference.
126968.m: A band dendrometer shows growth in thickness directly on the trunk.

126969.q: Why does a point dendrometer show the trunk shrinking and swelling over the course of a day?
a: The water content changes due to evaporation during the day
The tree only grows at night
The device expands in the sun
126969.e: During the day the tree loses a lot of water through its leaves, and the trunk shrinks slightly. At night its stores fill up again.
126969.m: Trunks shrink during the day and swell again at night.

126970.q: A tree has a circumference of 157 cm. Roughly what is its diameter?
126970.e: The diameter is the circumference divided by pi. 157 ÷ 3.14 gives about 50 cm.
126970.m: You get the diameter by dividing the circumference by pi.

126971.q: What is the traditional tool foresters use to measure trunk diameter called?
126971.e: The tree calliper works like a large sliding calliper. You place it around the trunk and read off the diameter directly.
126971.m: A tree calliper measures the diameter of a tree trunk.

126972.q: Which tissue produces the growth in thickness of a tree that dendrometers measure?
126972.e: The cambium is a thin layer of dividing cells under the bark. It produces wood towards the inside and phloem towards the outside.
126972.m: The cambium makes the tree trunk grow thicker.

126973.q: A tree has a diameter at breast height of 40 cm. Roughly what is its basal area?
126973.e: The basal area is pi times d² divided by 4. With d = 0.4 m this gives 3.14 times 0.16 ÷ 4, so about 0.126 m².
126973.m: The basal area is calculated like the area of a circle.

126974.q: What does dendrochronology study, unlike dendrometer measurements?
a: The sequence of tree ring widths over a long time
The current water flow in the trunk
126974.e: Dendrochronology reads tree rings in cores or wood and can look back centuries, for example to date timber buildings. Dendrometers, on the other hand, record the ongoing growth of living trees.
126974.m: Dendrochronology reads a tree’s history from its rings.

126975.q: What is measured with the eddy covariance method?
a: The exchange of CO2, water vapour and heat between an ecosystem and the air
The number of animals in a forest
126975.e: The method determines how much carbon dioxide a forest or meadow takes up or releases. At the same time it records evaporation and heat flows.
126975.m: Eddy covariance measures gas exchange between land and air.

126976.q: What principle is eddy covariance based on?
a: The link between vertical wind and gas concentration in air eddies
126976.e: Small air eddies carry air up and down. If rising air is on average poorer in CO2 than sinking air, the vegetation is taking up CO2.
126976.m: Air eddies reveal gas exchange between the ground and the atmosphere.

126977.q: Which two instruments are typical of an eddy covariance station?
a: Ultrasonic anemometer and fast gas analyser
126977.e: The ultrasonic anemometer measures wind in three directions very quickly. The gas analyser measures CO2 and water vapour at the same time.
126977.m: An eddy covariance station measures wind and gases at the same time and very quickly.

126978.q: Why does an eddy covariance station in a forest usually stand on a tower above the treetops?
a: It is meant to capture the air above the whole stand
So that animals do not damage the instruments
Because the air up there is still
So that satellites can see it
126978.e: The sensors have to measure above the treetops, where the air from the whole forest mixes. In this way the station records the gas exchange of a large area.
126978.m: Eddy covariance stations measure above the vegetation.

126979.q: An eddy covariance station shows that in summer a forest takes up more CO2 during the day than it releases. Which process is dominant then?
126979.e: During the day, the leaves bind more CO2 through photosynthesis than plants and soil organisms release through respiration. The station measures this net exchange.
126979.m: If photosynthesis dominates, an ecosystem takes up CO2 overall.

126980.q: In eddy covariance, what is the footprint?
a: The area from which the measured flows come
The base area of the measuring tower
The energy use of the instruments
126980.e: The station measures air that has passed over a certain area. This source area changes with wind direction, wind strength and measuring height.
126980.m: The footprint is the source area of the measured flows.

126981.q: Why are data from eddy covariance stations around the world brought together in a network?
a: To compare the CO2 exchange of different ecosystems
To produce weather reports for airports
126981.e: In the FLUXNET network, measurements from forests, meadows and fields on all continents are brought together. This shows how much CO2 ecosystems take up and how they react to heat or drought.
126981.m: FLUXNET compares the CO2 exchange of ecosystems worldwide.

126982.q: Why are night-time eddy covariance measurements often problematic?
a: In calm air there is too little turbulence
The instruments switch off at night
Plants do not breathe at night
It is too dark for the sensors
126982.e: On still nights a stable layer of air forms and CO2 collects near the ground. The station then underestimates the exchange, so such data are corrected or replaced.
126982.m: With weak turbulence, eddy covariance gives unreliable values.

127081.q: In which phase of a clinical drug trial is a new active substance typically first tested for tolerability on a small group of healthy volunteers?
127081.e: Phase I is mainly about safety, tolerability and how the substance behaves in the body. A small group of healthy volunteers is usually enough for this.
127081.m: Phase I first tests safety on a few people.

127082.q: Which trial phase usually includes hundreds to thousands of patients and provides the main basis for approving a medicine?
127082.e: Phase III compares the new remedy with a placebo or the standard therapy in many patients. Only large numbers show effectiveness and more common side effects reliably.
127082.m: Phase III is the big trial before approval.

127083.q: What are phase IV trials for?
a: Observation after approval, for example of rare side effects
First tests of a substance on cell cultures
Finding the right dose in a few patients
127083.e: Phase IV takes place after the medicine has been approved for the market. Because very many people now take it, rare side effects are noticed too.
127083.m: Phase IV monitors a medicine after approval.

127084.q: What is a trial called in which neither the participants nor the doctors know who is getting the real remedy and who a placebo?
127084.e: In a double-blind trial, neither the participants nor the treating doctors know who gets the real product (verum). This way, expectations do not influence the result.
127084.m: In a double-blind trial, neither participants nor doctors know who is in which group.

127085.q: Which body must give ethical approval for a study on humans in Switzerland before it starts?
127085.e: Under the Human Research Act, research on humans needs approval from the responsible ethics committee. Among other things, it examines benefits, risks and the protection of participants.
127085.m: No study on humans may start without approval from an ethics committee.

127086.q: What is the voluntary agreement to take part in a study called, given after being told about its aims, risks and procedure?
127086.e: Informed consent requires an explanation that is easy to understand. It can be withdrawn at any time without giving a reason.
127086.m: Anyone taking part in a study must give informed consent first.

127087.q: Which document of the World Medical Association sets out ethical principles for medical research on humans?
127087.e: The Declaration of Helsinki was adopted by the World Medical Association and has been revised several times since. Among other things, it requires informed consent and an independent ethical review.
127087.m: The Declaration of Helsinki is the ethical compass of research on humans.

127088.q: What is the control group in a clinical trial for?
a: For comparison with the group receiving the new treatment
127088.e: The control group receives a placebo or the existing standard therapy. Only by comparison can you tell whether the new treatment really works better.
127088.m: Without a comparison group, an effect cannot be proven with certainty.

a: Neither participants nor those treating them know who receives which treatment
The participants wear blindfolds during the trial
Two groups receive the same medicine in a double dose
The results are published twice independently
127089.e: In a double-blind trial, neither the test subjects nor the treating professionals know who is in which group. This way, expectations on both sides cannot distort the result.
127089.m: Double-blind means that patients and those treating them do not know who is in which group.

127090.q: What is a trial called in which only the participants do not know whether they are receiving the active substance or a placebo?
127090.e: In a single-blind trial, the study staff know who is in which group, but the test subjects do not. This protects against the placebo effect, but not against unconscious influence by those treating them.
127090.m: In a single-blind trial, only the participants do not know.

127091.q: Which bias is blinding the treating professionals mainly meant to prevent?
a: Their expectations influencing observation and assessment
Them publishing the study too early
127091.e: Anyone who knows who is getting the real remedy unconsciously judges symptoms differently or treats people differently. This is called observer or investigator bias.
127091.m: The professionals' expectations can also distort results.

127092.q: What is the random allocation of participants to the treatment and control groups called?
127092.e: In randomisation, chance decides the group. As a result, unknown influencing factors are also spread evenly over both groups.
127092.m: In randomisation, chance divides the participants into groups.

127093.q: What is it called when the blinding is lifted, for example when a person has serious side effects?
127093.e: In unblinding, it is revealed which treatment a person has received. This is necessary in an emergency so that doctors can act correctly.
127093.m: In an emergency, the blinding may be lifted by unblinding.

127094.q: Which type of study is considered the “gold standard” for proving that a therapy works?
127094.e: The randomised controlled trial, often carried out double-blind, minimises systematic errors best. That is why it is considered the gold standard of therapy research.
127094.m: Randomised controlled trials are considered the gold standard.

127095.q: In a triple-blind trial, who is blinded in addition to participants and those treating them?
a: The people who analyse the data
127095.e: In a triple-blind trial, the statisticians analysing the data do not know who is in which group either. This way, the analysis cannot be unconsciously steered.
127095.m: In a triple-blind trial, those analysing the data are blinded too.

127096.q: What does the Latin word “nocebo” literally mean?
127096.e: “Nocebo” comes from the Latin verb “nocere”, meaning to harm. “Placebo”, on the other hand, means “I shall please”.
127096.m: In Latin, nocebo means “I shall harm”.

127097.q: Which everyday situation is a typical example of the nocebo effect?
a: You read about side effects in the package leaflet and then notice them
You feel refreshed after a walk
You become immune after a vaccination
127097.e: Anyone who knows exactly which side effects are possible pays more attention to them and experiences them more often. This can even happen with a product that contains no active substance.
127097.m: Just reading about side effects can cause complaints.

127098.q: What does it show in many studies when people in the placebo group complain of side effects?
a: A nocebo effect, as they have not received any active substance
A mistake in producing the medicine
A delayed effect of the active substance
127098.e: The placebo group gets no active substance but often reports side effects similar to those of the verum group. These complaints come from expectations.
127098.m: Even a dummy pill can cause side effects because of expectations.

127099.q: Which measure can help reduce nocebo effects in medicine?
a: Keeping quiet about all side effects
A higher dose of the medicine
127099.e: Doctors must explain the risks, but they can do so in a balanced way, for example by stressing how many people tolerate the remedy well. The wording influences expectations.
127099.m: The way risks are explained influences how strongly nocebo effects occur.

127100.q: Which two psychological mechanisms are considered the main causes of the nocebo effect?
127100.e: Negative expectations, for example from explanations or other people's stories, and bad experiences in the past that have been learnt trigger nocebo reactions. This form of learning is called conditioning.
127100.m: Expectations and learnt experiences drive the nocebo effect.

127101.q: For which bodily sensation has the nocebo effect been researched particularly well?
127101.e: When test subjects expect more pain, they actually feel a stimulus as more painful. This can also be shown in brain activity.
127101.m: Expecting pain can make pain worse.

127102.q: What is the positive counterpart of the nocebo effect called?
127102.e: In the placebo effect, positive expectations improve how someone feels, even though no active substance is given. Both effects show how closely mind and body are linked.
127102.m: Positive expectations create the placebo effect, negative ones the nocebo effect.

127103.q: Which three elements does evidence-based medicine combine when deciding on treatment?
a: The best study evidence, clinical experience and the patient's wishes
Manufacturer's information, costs and waiting time
127103.e: Evidence-based medicine relies on the best available scientific evidence. This is combined with the professional's experience and the patient's values.
127103.m: Evidence-based medicine combines research, experience and the patient's wishes.

127104.q: Which kind of study is usually at the very top of the hierarchy of evidence?
a: A systematic review of randomised trials
A report on a single case
The opinion of a recognised expert
A laboratory experiment on cell cultures
127104.e: Systematic reviews combine all good studies on a question according to fixed rules. This means that chance findings from single studies carry less weight.
127104.m: Combined randomised trials provide the strongest evidence.

127105.q: What is the statistical combination of the results of several studies on the same question called?
127105.e: A meta-analysis combines the data of several studies into one overall result. This makes even small effects easier to detect with certainty.
127105.m: A meta-analysis combines many studies mathematically.

127106.q: Which international network is known for systematic reviews of medical treatments?
127106.e: Cochrane is an independent network of researchers that produces systematic reviews of therapies. These are considered an important basis of evidence-based medicine.
127106.m: Cochrane reviews summarise the study evidence on treatments.

127107.q: In a double-blind trial, what is known neither to the doctor nor to the test subject?
a: Who receives the medicine and who a placebo
127107.e: In a double-blind trial, neither those treating nor the test subjects know who gets the real remedy. This way, expectations do not influence the result.
127107.m: Double-blind trials protect against the influence of expectations.

127108.q: Which source is considered rather weak evidence in the hierarchy of evidence?
a: The opinion of a single expert without study data
127108.e: Expert opinions are based on experience, but not on comparative data collected systematically. That is why they are at the very bottom of the hierarchy.
127108.m: An opinion on its own is not yet strong proof.

127109.q: What are recommendations for treating particular diseases, drawn up by professional societies, called?
127109.e: Guidelines summarise the study evidence and give recommendations for diagnosis and therapy based on it. They are aids to decision-making, not rigid rules.
127109.m: Guidelines turn the study evidence into recommendations for everyday practice.

a: Studies with positive results are more likely to be published
Journals only print studies from Europe
Researchers only publish under a pseudonym
127110.e: If studies that show no effect appear less often, a therapy looks better in the literature than it really is. That is why studies should now be registered in advance.
127110.m: Unpublished negative studies distort the overall picture.

127111.q: A medicine lowers the risk of a heart attack from 10 % to 5 %. How many people must be treated so that, on average, one person has one heart attack fewer?
127111.e: The risk falls by 5 percentage points, that is for 5 out of 100 people. 100 divided by 5 makes 20. This number is called the number needed to treat (NNT).
127111.m: The NNT is the reciprocal of the absolute risk reduction.

127112.q: Apart from donation after primary brain death, which other form of organ donation is possible in Switzerland?
a: Donation without any confirmation of death
127112.e: All brain functions can also fail after a lasting cardiac arrest. Once this has been confirmed, organs can be removed.
127112.m: Organs can also be donated after a cardiac arrest.

127113.q: Under the extended opt-out system, what applies if there is no documented decision by the person who has died?
a: The relatives are asked and can refuse a donation
The organs are removed in any case
The hospital decides on its own
127113.e: “Extended” means that the next of kin are involved. They can refuse removal if this corresponds to what the person would presumably have wanted.
127113.m: Under the extended opt-out system, the relatives have a say.

127114.q: What is the transfer of organs or tissue from animals to humans called?
127114.e: The prefix “xeno” comes from Greek and means foreign. Because of the shortage of organs, research is being done with genetically modified pig organs, for example.
127114.m: In xenotransplantation, organs come from animals.

127115.q: Which rule applied to organ donation in Switzerland before the 2022 vote?
a: A duty to donate for everyone
127115.e: Until then, organs could only be removed if the person who had died or their relatives had agreed. So silence counted as a no.
127115.m: In the past, Switzerland required explicit consent.

127116.q: Which organ can a living person donate, because they can live well with the remaining one?
127116.e: People have two kidneys, and one healthy kidney is usually enough. Part of the liver can also be donated, because it grows back.
127116.m: A kidney can be donated during your lifetime.

127117.q: What is a transplant called in which donor and recipient are the same person, for example in a skin graft?
127117.e: In an autologous transplant, the body's own tissue is moved to another place. Because it comes from the person's own body, there is no rejection.
127117.m: Your own tissue is not rejected in an autologous transplant.

127118.q: Why is a transplanted cornea of the eye rejected less often than many other donor tissues?
a: It normally contains no blood vessels
It is frozen and boiled beforehand
127118.e: Without blood vessels, immune cells find it hard to reach the foreign tissue. That is why corneal transplants are among the most successful tissue transplants.
127118.m: The cornea, which has no blood vessels, is rarely rejected.

127119.q: What is the procedure called in which two donor-recipient pairs with incompatible kidneys swap their donor kidneys?
127119.e: If a donor's kidney does not match their own relative but does match another pair, the donations are crossed over. This way both recipients receive a compatible kidney.
127119.m: In crossover living donation, two pairs swap their donor kidneys.

127120.q: Which tissue features on cell surfaces are compared when looking for a matching donor organ or stem cell donor?
127120.e: HLA molecules (human leukocyte antigens) help the immune system tell the body's own cells from foreign ones. The more similar they are, the lower the risk of rejection.
127120.m: Matching HLA features lower the risk of rejection.

127121.q: How is brain death defined medically?
a: Irreversible loss of all functions of the cerebrum, cerebellum and brainstem
Loss of the cerebrum only, with the brainstem still working
The heart stopping for more than a minute
127121.e: In brain death, all brain functions have stopped for good, including the brainstem. A return to life is then impossible.
127121.m: Brain death means the final loss of the whole brain.

127122.q: Why can the heart of a brain-dead person keep beating in intensive care?
a: It has its own pacemaker, and the ventilator supplies oxygen
The brain still sends weak signals
The heart is massaged by hand from outside
Brain death never affects the circulation
127122.e: The sinus node produces the heartbeats itself, independently of the brain. As long as a machine provides ventilation, the heart gets enough oxygen.
127122.m: Thanks to the sinus node and ventilation, the heart keeps beating even after brain death.

127123.q: Which organisation issues the medical-ethical guidelines on determining death in Switzerland?
a: The Swiss Academy of Medical Sciences
127123.e: The SAMS writes guidelines on medical-ethical questions, including on determining death in organ donation. These guidelines are anchored in transplant law.
127123.m: The SAMS sets out how death is determined.

127124.q: Who may determine brain death in Switzerland in a possible organ donation?
a: Two qualified doctors who are not part of the transplant team
The relatives together with the hospital director
127124.e: Death is determined according to the four-eyes principle by two independent, qualified doctors. They may not be involved in either the removal or the transplant.
127124.m: Independent experts determine brain death, not the transplant team.

127125.q: What is tested in the apnoea test as part of diagnosing brain death?
a: Whether the person still starts breathing on their own when carbon dioxide is raised
Whether the heart beats without medicines
Whether the pupils are the same size
127125.e: A high level of carbon dioxide in the blood is the strongest stimulus to breathe, controlled by the brainstem. If no breathing starts even so, the breathing centre has failed.
127125.m: The apnoea test checks whether the brainstem still triggers breathing.

127126.q: Which reflex is one of the brainstem reflexes tested when diagnosing brain death?
127126.e: In the corneal reflex, the eye closes when the cornea is touched. It is controlled by the brainstem. Knee-jerk reflexes, by contrast, run through the spinal cord and can remain in brain death.
127126.m: Missing brainstem reflexes are a sign of brain death.

127127.q: How does a vegetative state differ from brain death?
a: In a vegetative state the brainstem still works, for example for breathing
In a vegetative state the whole brain has failed
In a vegetative state the heart no longer beats
127127.e: In a vegetative state, mainly the functions of the cerebrum are severely disturbed, but the brainstem works. Those affected usually breathe on their own and are alive; in brain death this is not the case.
127127.m: In a vegetative state the person is alive; in brain death they are dead.

127128.q: Which faculty first set out influential criteria in 1968 for the “irreversible coma” that is now considered brain death?
a: The Faculty of Medicine of the University of Basel
127128.e: In 1968, an ad hoc committee of Harvard Medical School drew up criteria for irreversible coma. These shaped the worldwide definition of brain death.
127128.m: The Harvard criteria of 1968 shaped the concept of brain death.

127129.q: What do you set out in a living will?
a: Which medical measures you agree to or refuse if you can no longer make decisions
Who inherits your wealth after your death
How the funeral should be held
127129.e: A living will applies in case you can no longer decide for yourself. Doctors must in principle follow it.
127129.m: A living will says what should happen medically if you can no longer decide.

127130.q: In which law is the living will regulated in Switzerland?
127130.e: Since the new adult protection law, the living will has been anchored in the Civil Code. It also states which formal requirements apply.
127130.m: The living will is in the Swiss Civil Code.

127131.q: Which condition must a person meet to write a valid living will?
a: They must be capable of judgement
They must be of age and married
They must already be seriously ill
127131.e: Under the Civil Code, a person who is capable of judgement can draw up a living will. So they must be able to understand what they are setting out.
127131.m: Only someone capable of judgement can draw up a living will.

127132.q: Which form does Swiss law require for a living will?
a: Spoken in front of two witnesses
127132.e: A living will must be drawn up in writing, dated and signed. It may be written on a computer or be a form; certification by a notary is not needed.
127132.m: A living will must be in writing, dated and signed.

127133.q: In addition to the measures you want, what else can you decide in a living will?
a: A person you trust who makes medical decisions for you
The amount of the health insurance premium
127133.e: You can name a person who discusses the treatment with the doctors and decides. They should act in the way the author of the living will would want.
127133.m: In a living will you can name a person to represent you.

127134.q: Where in Switzerland can you have it noted that a living will exists and where it is kept?
127134.e: The Civil Code provides that you can have its existence and where it is kept entered on your insurance card. This way, professionals find the living will faster in an emergency.
127134.m: A note on the insurance card helps people find the living will.

127135.q: Can you change or cancel a living will?
a: Yes, at any time, as long as you are capable of judgement
127135.e: A living will can be changed or revoked at any time, for example by destroying it or writing a new one. It is recommended to check it regularly.
127135.m: A living will can be changed at any time.

127136.q: Unlike the living will, which instrument also covers financial matters and legal transactions if you lose the capacity of judgement?
127136.e: With the advance care directive, you give a person responsibility for your personal care, your finances and representing you in legal matters. It must be handwritten or publicly certified.
127136.m: The advance care directive covers more than just medical questions.

127137.q: Which surgical system is the best-known example of robot-assisted surgery?
127137.e: The da Vinci system has been used around the world for about two decades, including in many Swiss hospitals. It is named after Leonardo da Vinci.
127137.m: The da Vinci system is the best-known surgical robot.

127138.q: In a typical robot-assisted operation, who guides the movements of the instruments?
a: The surgeon, using a control console
The robot, completely on its own
The nurse at the operating table
127138.e: The surgeon sits at a console and controls the robot arms with hand grips and pedals. The robot passes on the movements but does not decide anything itself.
127138.m: In robot-assisted surgery, a human is always in control.

127139.q: Which type of operation do most robot-assisted operations belong to?
a: Minimally invasive operations through small incisions
Open operations with a large abdominal incision
Operations with no anaesthetic at all
Operations without any opening in the skin
127139.e: The instruments are inserted into the body through a few small openings. This can reduce pain, blood loss and recovery time.
127139.m: Robot-assisted operations are usually minimally invasive.

127140.q: What advantage does the tremor filtering of a surgical robot offer?
a: It cancels out slight trembling of the hands
It cools the tissue during the cut
127140.e: The software detects small, involuntary trembling movements and does not pass them on to the instruments. This makes very steady, precise movements possible.
127140.m: Tremor filtering makes trembling movements harmless.

127141.q: A surgical robot scales movements in the ratio 3 to 1. How far does the tip of the instrument move if the surgeon's hand moves 4.5 cm?
127141.e: With a scaling of 3 to 1, the hand movement is divided by 3: 4.5 cm / 3 = 1.5 cm. This allows very fine movements.
127141.m: Motion scaling turns large hand movements into fine instrument movements.

127142.q: What is considered a disadvantage of many robot-assisted surgical systems?
a: High costs and a limited sense of touch
Greater blood loss compared with open operations
127142.e: Buying and maintaining the systems is very expensive. In addition, the surgeon hardly feels the resistance of the tissue directly, because there is often no haptic feedback.
127142.m: Surgical robots are expensive and give little sense of touch.

a: A surgeon operates via a robot from a great distance
An operation is broadcast on television
A doctor advises patients by telephone
A robot operates without any humans at all
127143.e: In telesurgery, the surgeon sits at a console far away from the operating theatre. In 2001, a surgeon in New York controlled a robot that operated on a patient in Strasbourg.
127143.m: With telesurgery, you can operate over great distances.

127144.q: Why are minimally invasive operations also called keyhole surgery?
a: Because the operation is done through very small openings
Because only the head is operated on
Because the operating theatre is locked
Because the instruments look like keys
127144.e: The camera and instruments are guided into the body through a few small incisions. The openings are hardly bigger than a keyhole.
127144.m: Keyhole surgery manages with small incisions.

127145.q: What does occupational medicine deal with?
a: The interactions between work and health
127145.e: Occupational medicine studies how working conditions affect health. It aims to prevent occupational diseases and accidents at work.
127145.m: Occupational medicine protects health at the workplace.

127146.q: From the point of view of occupational medicine, which question should a doctor ask every patient?
a: What music do you like listening to?
127146.e: Even the founder of occupational medicine, Bernardino Ramazzini, recommended asking about the job around 1700. Many illnesses are linked to dust, noise or strain at the workplace.
127146.m: Your job can be the key to an illness.

127147.q: Which insurance covers recognised occupational diseases in Switzerland?
127147.e: Under the Accident Insurance Act, occupational diseases are treated the same as accidents at work. That is why accident insurance, such as Suva, pays.
127147.m: In Switzerland, occupational diseases are covered by accident insurance.

127148.q: Which malignant disease of the lining of the chest or abdomen is typically caused by breathing in asbestos dust?
127148.e: Asbestos fibres get into the lungs and as far as the lining of the chest, where they can cause a mesothelioma decades later. Asbestos has long been banned in Switzerland, but old buildings still contain it.
127148.m: Asbestos can cause a mesothelioma even decades later.

127149.q: Which lung disease threatens tunnel miners who breathe in quartz dust?
127149.e: Fine quartz dust scars the lung tissue permanently. Silicosis (dust lung) used to be one of the most common occupational diseases in mining and tunnel building.
127149.m: Quartz dust can scar the lungs and cause silicosis.

127150.q: Which occupational disease is caused by years of loud noise at the workplace?
127150.e: Constant noise damages the hair cells in the inner ear, which do not renew themselves. Hearing protection can prevent this permanent hearing loss.
127150.m: Noise damages hearing permanently, so hearing protection is a must.

127151.q: What does the MAK value indicate?
a: The maximum permitted concentration of a harmful substance in the air at the workplace
The maximum working time per week
The minimum wage in a canton
The permitted body temperature at work
127151.e: MAK stands for maximum workplace concentration. Up to this value, according to current knowledge, a substance is considered harmless to health during normal working hours.
127151.m: The MAK value limits harmful substances in the air at the workplace.

127152.q: Which federal law in Switzerland regulates working and rest times as well as health protection in companies, among other things?
127152.e: The Labour Act contains rules on working hours, breaks, night work and health protection. Together with the Accident Insurance Act, it is decisive for many companies.
127152.m: The Labour Act protects employees from working hours that are too long.

127153.q: What is the aim of ergonomics?
a: To adapt people to every machine
To achieve as many working hours as possible
To measure the energy use of devices
127153.e: Ergonomics designs workplaces, tools and procedures so that they suit human abilities. This protects health and increases performance.

127154.q: Which Greek words make up the term “ergonomics”?
a: Ergon for work and nomos for law
Ergon for energy and nomos for name
Ergon for body and nomos for movement
Ergon for tool and nomos for house
127154.e: “Ergon” means work or deed, “nomos” means law or rule. So ergonomics is the study of the laws of work.
127154.m: Ergonomics literally means the study of work.

127155.q: At roughly what height should the top edge of the screen be at an ergonomic workstation?
a: At eye level or slightly below
At the height of your belly button
At the height of the edge of the desk
127155.e: If the top edge is at about eye level, you look slightly downwards. This takes the strain off your neck and reduces dry eyes.
127155.m: The screen belongs at about eye level.

127156.q: What is the study of measuring the human body called, which is used for designing chairs and tables, for example?
127156.e: Anthropometry records body measurements such as leg length or shoulder width. With these data, workplaces are designed to suit as many people as possible.
127156.m: Anthropometry provides the body measurements for ergonomic furniture.

127157.q: How should a screen be positioned in relation to the window to avoid glare?
a: Side on, so that you look parallel to the window
With your back directly to the window
Directly in front of the window, looking out
127157.e: If the screen is at right angles to the window, daylight falls in from the side. This way there are no reflections on the screen and no big differences in brightness in your field of vision.
127157.m: It is best to look at the screen parallel to the window.

127158.q: What is recommended for long periods of work sitting down?
a: Change position often and stand up now and then
Sit in the same way all day if possible
Only sit on the front edge of the chair
Always bend your back strongly forwards
127158.e: The body is built for movement; even the best sitting posture puts strain on it over time. Dynamic sitting and switching between sitting and standing relieve the muscles and the intervertebral discs.
127158.m: The best posture is the next posture.

127159.q: Roughly what level of lighting is recommended for reading and writing work in an office?
127159.e: Workplace standards give about 500 lux for office work involving reading and writing. Too little light tires the eyes, too much dazzles.
127159.m: Good office work needs about 500 lux of light.

127160.q: Roughly what angle is recommended for the elbows and knees when sitting ergonomically at a desk?
127160.e: With your elbows at roughly a right angle, your forearms rest loosely on the desk. Knees at a right angle with your feet flat on the floor take the strain off your thighs and back.
127160.m: When sitting, your elbows and knees form roughly a right angle.

127161.q: What does the so-called 20-20-20 rule recommend for screen work?
a: Every 20 minutes, look about 6 metres away for 20 seconds
Every 20 minutes, switch off the screen for 20 seconds
Lower the screen by 20 centimetres and tilt it by 20 degrees
Every 20 minutes, close your eyes for 20 seconds
127161.e: The rule speaks of 20 feet, which is about 6 metres. Looking into the distance relaxes the eye muscles, which are constantly tense when you look at things close up.
127161.m: A quick look into the distance relaxes the eyes.

127162.q: What is the technical term for complaints such as mouse arm that are caused by repeated strain?
127162.e: RSI means an injury caused by repeated strain. The term covers complaints in muscles, tendons and nerves that come from monotonous movements.
127162.m: Mouse arm is one of the Repetitive Strain Injuries.

127163.q: What is the main cause of mouse arm?
a: Many small, identical movements in a rigid posture
A single fall onto the hand
127163.e: Hours of clicking and scrolling always strain the same muscles and tendons. Together with a static posture and few breaks, this leads to overuse complaints.
127163.m: Monotonous movements without breaks cause mouse arm.

127164.q: Which complaints are typical of mouse arm?
a: Pain, tingling and loss of strength in the hand, arm or shoulder
127164.e: At first the complaints often only appear during work. If the strain continues, they can become permanent.
127164.m: Mouse arm shows itself through pain and tingling in the arm.

127165.q: Which measure helps prevent mouse arm?
a: Regular short breaks and varied movements
Keeping the mouse as far from the body as possible
Never resting the arm while working
127165.e: Short breaks, stretching exercises and switching between the mouse and keyboard shortcuts relieve the strain. It is also important to keep the mouse close to the body.
127165.m: Breaks and variety protect against mouse arm.

127166.q: What advantage does a vertical mouse offer?
a: The forearm stays in a natural handshake position
127166.e: With a normal mouse the forearm is twisted inwards, which strains muscles and tendons. The vertical shape keeps the hand upright, as when shaking hands.
127166.m: A vertical mouse keeps the forearm in a relaxed position.

127167.q: Which inflammation can be caused by constantly repeated hand and finger movements and is often linked to mouse arm?
127167.e: Tendons glide inside protective tendon sheaths. If they are overloaded, these sheaths can become inflamed, which hurts when you move.

127168.q: In which condition is the median nerve squeezed in the wrist, causing tingling in the fingers?
127168.e: The median nerve runs through the narrow carpal tunnel at the base of the hand. If it is squeezed there, the thumb, index and middle fingers in particular tingle.
127168.m: In carpal tunnel syndrome a nerve in the wrist is trapped.

127169.q: What is the name of the painful irritation of the tendon attachments on the outer elbow, which can also be caused by a lot of mouse work?
127169.e: In tennis elbow the attachments of the forearm extensor muscles on the outer elbow are overloaded. These muscles also work constantly when you hold and click a mouse.
127169.m: You can get tennis elbow without playing tennis.

127170.q: What does the abbreviation Suva stand for?
127170.e: Suva is the largest accident insurer in Switzerland. It mainly insures employees in industry, trade and construction.
127170.m: Suva is the Swiss National Accident Insurance Fund.

127171.q: In which city does Suva have its headquarters?
127171.e: Suva's headquarters are in Lucerne. It also has agencies all over Switzerland.
127171.m: Suva has its headquarters in Lucerne.

127172.q: Which three areas does Suva cover as an accident insurer?
a: Occupational accidents, non-occupational accidents and occupational diseases
127172.e: Compulsory accident insurance under the Accident Insurance Act (UVG) covers accidents at work and in your free time, as well as occupational diseases. Ordinary illnesses are covered by health insurance.
127172.m: Suva insures accidents and occupational diseases.

127173.q: From how many working hours per week with the same employer are employees in Switzerland also insured against non-occupational accidents?
127173.e: Anyone who works at least eight hours a week for the same employer is also compulsorily insured for accidents in their free time. Below that, only occupational accidents are covered.
127173.m: From eight hours a week, accidents in your free time are insured too.

127174.q: What percentage of the insured earnings is the daily allowance from accident insurance if you are completely unable to work?
127174.e: Under the Accident Insurance Act, the daily allowance for complete inability to work is 80 per cent of the insured earnings. It is paid after a short waiting period.
127174.m: The UVG daily allowance is 80 per cent of the insured wage.

127175.q: Who is represented on the Suva Council, Suva's highest governing body?
127175.e: The Suva Council has 40 seats: 16 for employers' organisations, 16 for employees' organisations and 8 for the Confederation. Its members are elected by the Federal Council for four years (term of office 2024 to 2027).
127175.m: Employers, employees and the Confederation sit on the Suva Council.

127176.q: Since Suva is not profit-oriented, what happens to its surpluses?
a: They flow back to the insured through lower premiums
They are paid out to shareholders as dividends
They go to the federal treasury
They are invested in gold and never used
127176.e: Suva is an independent company under public law with no profit goal. It passes on surpluses in the form of premium reductions.
127176.m: Suva returns profits through lower premiums.

127177.q: What task does Suva take on in addition to insurance?
a: Prevention of accidents and occupational diseases
127177.e: Suva advises companies, runs campaigns and checks safety at work in many industries. Prevention, insurance and rehabilitation are its three pillars.
127177.m: Suva prevents accidents through prevention work.

127178.q: Why does Suva run its own rehabilitation clinics?
a: To prepare accident victims for their return to everyday life and work
127178.e: In its rehab clinics, people who have had serious accidents do targeted training. The aim is for them to be able to live and work independently again.
127178.m: Suva rehab clinics help accident victims back into everyday life and work.

127179.q: In which scientific journal did Einstein publish his groundbreaking papers of 1905?
127179.e: “Annalen der Physik” was one of the leading journals at the time. Max Planck was the journal's adviser responsible for theoretical contributions.
127179.m: Einstein's 1905 papers appeared in “Annalen der Physik”.

127180.q: A spaceship is 100 m long at rest. How long does it appear to an observer at rest if its Lorentz factor γ equals 2?
127180.e: Length contraction is L = L₀ / γ. So 100 m / 2 = 50 m in the direction of flight.
127180.m: Fast-moving bodies appear shortened in the direction of motion.

127181.q: For which work did Einstein receive the Nobel Prize in Physics?
a: For the general theory of relativity
127181.e: Einstein received the Nobel Prize for 1921 for his explanation of the photoelectric effect using light quanta. The theory of relativity was still controversial at the time.
127181.m: Einstein got the Nobel Prize for the photoelectric effect.

127182.q: Which everyday technology has to take effects of relativity into account to work accurately?
127182.e: Because of their speed and the weaker gravity, the clocks in navigation satellites run differently from clocks on Earth. Without correction, positions would shift by kilometres every day.
127182.m: Without relativity GPS would be inaccurate.

127183.q: According to general relativity, does a very precise clock on the Jungfraujoch run faster or slower than one in Interlaken?
a: Faster, because gravity there is slightly weaker
Slower, because the air there is thinner
Just as fast, height makes no difference
Slower, because it is colder there
127183.e: The deeper you are in a gravitational field, the more slowly time passes. The difference is tiny but can be measured with atomic clocks.
127183.m: Time passes more slowly in stronger gravity.

a: A state near absolute zero in which many particles behave like a single one
A very hot gas of ions and electrons
A water droplet in a cloud
A substance between liquid and crystalline
127184.e: Einstein and Bose predicted this state of matter in the 1920s. At extremely low temperatures many particles take on the same quantum state. It was first produced in 1995.
127184.m: A Bose-Einstein condensate forms near absolute zero.

127185.q: Which household appliance without moving parts did Einstein patent together with Leó Szilárd?
127185.e: The Einstein-Szilárd refrigerator worked by absorption and needed neither motor nor compressor. It was meant to be safer than the devices of the time with poisonous coolants.

127186.q: At which Swiss university did Einstein study and later also become a professor?
127186.e: Einstein studied at the Polytechnic, today's ETH Zurich, and graduated in 1900. In 1912 he returned there as a professor.
127186.m: Einstein studied and taught at ETH Zurich.

127187.q: Which long-puzzling anomaly in a planet's orbit was Einstein able to explain with his theory of gravity?
127187.e: The point of Mercury's orbit closest to the Sun moves slightly faster than Newton's theory predicts. General relativity explains exactly this remainder.
127187.m: Mercury's orbit was an early success of general relativity.

127188.q: Which city did Einstein move to in 1914 to work at the Prussian Academy of Sciences?
127188.e: In Berlin Einstein became a member of the Academy and could devote himself fully to research. There he completed the general theory of relativity.
127188.m: From 1914 Einstein did his research in Berlin.

127189.q: What does the Pauli principle say about electrons in an atom?
a: No two electrons have all the same quantum numbers
All electrons have the same spin
127189.e: The exclusion principle forbids two electrons from occupying exactly the same quantum state. It explains the shell structure of atoms and therefore the periodic table.
127189.m: Two electrons may never be in the same quantum state.

127190.q: Which physicist gave the light, neutral particle proposed by Pauli its present name?
127190.e: Pauli first called his particle the “neutron”. When the heavy neutron was discovered in 1932, Fermi coined the Italian diminutive “neutrino”.
127190.m: Fermi named Pauli's particle the neutrino.

127192.q: What did Wolfgang Pauli receive the Nobel Prize in Physics for in 1945?
a: For building the first nuclear reactor
127192.e: The Pauli principle explains why electrons fill the shells of an atom one after another. For this Pauli was awarded the Nobel Prize in 1945.
127192.m: Pauli received the Nobel Prize for the exclusion principle.

127193.q: On which subject did Pauli, as a student of about 21, write a review article that Einstein praised highly?
127193.e: Pauli wrote the article for the “Encyclopaedia of Mathematical Sciences”. For a long time it was regarded as one of the best accounts of the theory of relativity.
127193.m: Even as a student Pauli wrote a standard work on relativity.

127194.q: Which particle did Pauli predict in 1930 to save the energy balance in beta decay?
127194.e: In beta decay some energy seemed to be missing. Pauli proposed an invisible, neutral particle that carries the missing energy away. It was only detected in 1956.

127195.q: Where did Pauli spend much of the Second World War?
127195.e: Pauli feared that Switzerland would be occupied and went to the Institute for Advanced Study in Princeton in 1940. After the war he returned to Zurich.
127195.m: During the war Pauli did research in Princeton.

127196.q: What did physicists jokingly mean by the “Pauli effect”?
a: That experiments failed when Pauli was nearby
That Pauli could solve any calculation in his head
That clocks ran faster near Pauli
That Pauli never missed a lecture
127196.e: Pauli was a pure theorist. Colleagues claimed in jest that equipment broke as soon as he entered a laboratory.
127196.m: The Pauli effect is a joking anecdote about broken experiments.

127197.q: Which Swiss city did Daniel Bernoulli's famous family of scholars come from?
127197.e: The Bernoulli family produced several important mathematicians in Basel, including Jakob, Johann and Daniel Bernoulli. Daniel taught at the University of Basel.
127197.m: The Bernoullis were a family of scholars from Basel.

127198.q: What is the dynamic pressure ½ρv² of air (ρ about 1.2 kg/m³) flowing at 10 m/s?
127198.e: ½ · 1.2 kg/m³ · (10 m/s)² = 0.6 · 100 Pa = 60 Pa. This dynamic pressure is one term of the Bernoulli equation.
127198.m: Dynamic pressure grows with the square of the speed.

127199.q: What relationship does Bernoulli's law describe for a flow?
a: Where the flow is faster, the pressure is lower
Where the flow is faster, the pressure is higher
The pressure does not depend on the speed
127199.e: The Bernoulli equation follows from conservation of energy. When the fluid gains kinetic energy, the static pressure falls.

127200.q: What idea did Daniel Bernoulli hold about the motion of a vibrating string?
a: It can be described as a superposition of simple sine oscillations
It always vibrates at one single frequency
It only vibrates as long as you touch it
127200.e: Bernoulli recognised that the vibration is made up of a fundamental tone and overtones. This superposition principle was later developed mathematically through Fourier analysis.
127200.m: A string's vibration is a sum of fundamental and overtones.

127201.q: According to Torricelli's law, how fast does water flow out of a small hole 5 m below the water surface (g equal to 10 m/s²)?
127201.e: From the Bernoulli equation, v = √(2gh). So √(2 · 10 m/s² · 5 m) = √100 m/s = 10 m/s.
127201.m: The outflow speed grows with the square root of the water depth.

127202.q: Which instrument on aircraft determines airspeed from the dynamic pressure of the oncoming air?
127202.e: The Pitot tube compares the total pressure at its tip with the static pressure. From the difference, Bernoulli's law gives the speed.
127202.m: A Pitot tube measures speed using dynamic pressure.

127203.q: Under which conditions does the simple form of the Bernoulli equation hold strictly?
a: For frictionless, incompressible and steady flows
Only for gases at very high temperature
Only for turbulent flows with eddies
127203.e: The equation follows from conservation of energy along a streamline. Friction, compression and changes over time are neglected.
127203.m: The simple Bernoulli equation applies to ideal flows.

127204.q: Water (ρ equal to 1000 kg/m³) flows in a horizontal pipe first at 1 m/s, then at 3 m/s. By how much does the static pressure fall according to Bernoulli?
127204.e: Δp = ½ · ρ · (v₂² minus v₁²) = 0.5 · 1000 · (9 minus 1) Pa = 4000 Pa. The kinetic energy gained comes at the expense of pressure.
127204.m: In a horizontal flow the pressure falls when the speed rises.

127205.q: A fair coin is tossed 10,000 times. What does the law of large numbers, proved by Jakob I Bernoulli, say?
a: The share of heads is very probably close to 50 per cent
After many tails, heads will come soon
The share of heads varies more and more
127205.e: With many repetitions the relative frequency approaches the probability. But an exact result is not guaranteed, and the coin has no memory.
127205.m: With many trials the relative frequency approaches the probability.

127206.q: Which curve, shaped like a figure eight lying on its side, is named after Jakob I Bernoulli?
127206.e: Bernoulli's lemniscate looks like a figure eight lying on its side. It resembles the symbol for infinity.
127206.m: Bernoulli's lemniscate is a sideways figure eight.

127207.q: What is the probability of getting exactly two heads in three tosses of a fair coin?
127207.e: There are 2³ = 8 equally likely outcomes, and 3 of them have exactly two heads (HHT, HTH, THH). Such series of trials are called Bernoulli processes.
