127207.m: A Bernoulli process consists of independent trials with two outcomes.

127208.q: Which curve is the solution to the brachistochrone problem, which Jakob I Bernoulli also solved in 1697?
127208.e: The task was to find the path along which a body slides fastest between two points under gravity. It is not a straight line but part of a cycloid.
127208.m: The fastest slide has the shape of a cycloid.

127209.q: Which curve describes a freely hanging rope, whose shape Jakob I Bernoulli set as a problem in 1690?
127209.e: Galileo had guessed that a hanging rope forms a parabola. Leibniz, Huygens and Johann Bernoulli showed that it is the catenary, which can be described with the hyperbolic cosine function.
127209.m: A hanging rope forms a catenary, not a parabola.

127210.q: At which university did Jakob I Bernoulli teach as professor of mathematics from 1687?
127210.e: Jakob I Bernoulli came from Basel and taught at its university until his death in 1705. The Bernoulli family produced several important mathematicians.
127210.m: Jakob I Bernoulli was professor of mathematics in Basel.

127211.q: What is the probability of not rolling a single six in four rolls of a fair die?
127211.e: Each roll is a Bernoulli trial with probability 5/6 for “no six”. (5/6)⁴ = 625/1296 ≈ 0.482, so about 48 %.
127211.m: For independent trials you multiply the probabilities.

127212.q: On average, how many sixes do you expect in 60 rolls of a fair die?
127212.e: For a Bernoulli process the expected value is E = n · p. So 60 · 1/6 = 10.
127212.m: The expected value of a Bernoulli process is number of trials times probability.

127213.q: Which ruler brought Leonhard Euler to the Academy in Berlin in 1741?
127213.e: Frederick II, also called Frederick the Great, wanted to strengthen the Berlin Academy. Euler stayed in Berlin for about 25 years.
127213.m: Frederick the Great brought Euler to Berlin.

127214.q: What do Euler's equations of fluid dynamics describe?
a: The orbits of planets around the Sun
The spread of light in glass
127214.e: The Euler equations describe flows without internal friction. With friction they are extended to the Navier-Stokes equations.
127214.m: The Euler equations describe ideal flows.

127215.q: What do you calculate with Euler's buckling formula?
a: The load at which a slender rod buckles sideways
The bending of a light ray in a prism
127215.e: The critical buckling load depends on the material, cross-section, length and support of the rod. It is important in civil engineering but applies only to slender, elastic rods.
127215.m: Euler's buckling formula says when a slender rod buckles.

127216.q: Which famous number with a value of about 2.718 is named after Leonhard Euler?
127216.e: Euler's number e is the base of the natural logarithm. It turns up everywhere in growth and decay processes.

127217.q: What is the famous formula e^(iπ) + 1 = 0, which links five important numbers in mathematics, called?
127217.e: Euler's identity links e, i, π, 1 and 0 in a single equation. Many consider it one of the most beautiful formulas in mathematics.
127217.m: Euler's identity links e, i, π, 1 and 0.

127218.q: In 1735 Euler solved the “Basel problem”. What was being looked for?
a: The sum of the reciprocals of all square numbers
127218.e: The task was the sum 1 + 1/4 + 1/9 + 1/16 + ... Euler showed that it is exactly π²/6, about 1.645.
127218.m: The Basel problem asks for the sum of the reciprocals of the square numbers.

127219.q: What is the simplest numerical method for solving a differential equation approximately step by step called?
127219.e: In the explicit Euler method you start from an initial value and follow the slope in small steps. It is simple but inaccurate with large steps.
127219.m: The Euler method solves differential equations in small steps.

127220.q: In mechanics, which three angles are used to describe the orientation of a rotating rigid body in space?
127220.e: The three Euler angles give rotations about certain axes carried out one after another. They can be used, for example, to describe the orientation of a gyroscope or a satellite.
127220.m: Three Euler angles fix the orientation of a body.

127221.q: In 1736 Euler studied the problem of the Seven Bridges of Königsberg. What was the question?
a: Whether you can cross every bridge exactly once
How much load each bridge can carry
How fast the river flows under the bridges
127221.e: Euler proved that such a walk is not possible. In doing so he laid the foundation of graph theory.
127221.m: With the Königsberg bridges Euler founded graph theory.

127222.q: What did Auguste Piccard mainly want to study with his stratosphere flights?
a: The Earth's magnetic field at the North Pole
127222.e: At high altitude cosmic radiation is stronger because the atmosphere has not yet weakened it. Piccard wanted to measure it there.
127222.m: Piccard flew high to measure cosmic radiation.

127223.q: What was special about the gondola of Auguste Piccard's stratosphere balloon?
a: It was an airtight, sealed pressure cabin
It was open like a balloon basket
It had its own propeller engine
127223.e: At about 16 km altitude the air pressure is so low that you cannot survive without protection. Piccard therefore built a spherical, pressure-tight aluminium gondola, a model for later aircraft cabins.
127223.m: Piccard flew into the stratosphere in a pressurised gondola.

127224.q: In which submersible, built on Piccard's principle, did Jacques Piccard and Don Walsh reach the deepest point of the Mariana Trench in 1960?
127224.e: The Trieste was developed by Auguste Piccard and his son Jacques. It dived to almost 11,000 m in the Challenger Deep.
127224.m: In 1960 the Trieste reached the deepest point of the oceans.

127225.q: Why does a hydrogen-filled balloon like Piccard's rise in the air?
a: Because the buoyancy is greater than the weight of balloon, gas and load
Because hydrogen is attracted by the Sun
Because the Earth repels the balloon magnetically
127225.e: According to Archimedes' principle, the buoyancy equals the weight of the air displaced. Hydrogen is much lighter than air, so this buoyancy can exceed the total weight.
127225.m: A gas balloon rises as long as its buoyancy is greater than its weight.

127226.q: Why was Piccard's stratosphere balloon only partly filled with gas at launch?
a: Because the gas expands greatly as the air pressure falls at altitude
Because the gas was too expensive at launch
Because a full balloon cannot take off
Because the gas contracts in the cold and then bursts
127226.e: As altitude increases, the outside air pressure falls sharply and the gas in the balloon needs more space. A balloon full at launch would tear at altitude.
127226.m: A high-altitude balloon starts limp and is only fully inflated high up.

127227.q: Compared with the pressure at sea level, what is the air pressure at about 16 km altitude, which Piccard reached in 1931?
127227.e: Air pressure roughly halves every 5 to 6 kilometres. At about 16 km it is therefore only about 100 hPa instead of about 1000 hPa.
127227.m: In the stratosphere the air pressure is only a fraction.

127228.q: By what factor does an amount of gas expand at constant temperature if the outside pressure falls to a fifth?
127228.e: According to Boyle's law, p · V = constant. If the pressure falls to a fifth, the volume becomes five times as large.
127228.m: At constant temperature, the pressure and volume of a gas are inversely proportional.

127229.q: Roughly what water pressure is there at 11 km depth in the sea, where Piccard's submersible principle had its greatest success (ρ equal to 1000 kg/m³, g equal to 10 m/s²)?
127229.e: p = ρ · g · h = 1000 · 10 · 11,000 Pa = 1.1 · 10⁸ Pa. Since 1 bar is 10⁵ Pa, that gives about 1100 bar.
127229.m: For every 10 metres of water depth the pressure rises by about 1 bar.

127230.q: What did Fritz Zwicky suspect in 1933 because the galaxies in the Coma Cluster were moving much too fast?
a: The cluster is made of antimatter
The galaxies are accelerated by dark energy
The speed of light is greater there
127230.e: The visible mass was nowhere near enough to hold the fast galaxies together. Zwicky concluded there was a lot of invisible mass, which he called “dark matter”.
127230.m: Zwicky gave dark matter its name.

127231.q: Which extremely dense stellar remnants did Fritz Zwicky and Walter Baade predict in 1934 as a result of supernovae?
127231.e: Zwicky and Baade suspected that in a supernova a star collapses into a tiny body of neutrons. Neutron stars were only detected in 1967, as pulsars.

127232.q: Which hypothesis did Zwicky put forward in 1929 as an alternative explanation for the redshift of distant galaxies?
a: Light loses energy over long distances (“tired light”)
Light is coloured red by planets
The Earth moves faster than light
127232.e: Zwicky suspected that light grows “tired” on its long journey and therefore redder. This idea is now considered disproved; the redshift is explained by the expansion of the universe.
127232.m: The tired light hypothesis did not hold up.

127233.q: Which extensive catalogue did Zwicky compile with colleagues at the Palomar Observatory?
a: A catalogue of galaxies and galaxy clusters
127233.e: The catalogue, published in several volumes, lists tens of thousands of galaxies and thousands of galaxy clusters. For a long time it was an important tool in astronomy.
127233.m: Zwicky catalogued tens of thousands of galaxies.

127234.q: Which citizenship did Fritz Zwicky keep all his life, although he was born in Bulgaria and did research in California?
127234.e: Zwicky was a citizen of Mollis in the canton of Glarus and grew up there in part. Despite his long time in the USA he always remained Swiss.
127234.m: Fritz Zwicky was an astronomer from Glarus.

127235.q: In which technical field did Zwicky also work during the Second World War?
127235.e: Zwicky was director of research at a rocket propulsion company in California. He was regarded as a pioneer of jet propulsion.

127236.q: What is the ring-shaped image of a light source called when it lies exactly behind a gravitational lens?
127236.e: If source, lens and observer lie exactly in a line, the light is bent equally all round. A glowing ring appears.
127236.m: With perfect alignment a gravitational lens creates an Einstein ring.

127237.q: Which sky survey project at the Palomar Observatory, which searches for short-lived events in the sky, bears Zwicky's name?
127237.e: The facility uses a large camera on the Samuel Oschin Telescope and searches, among other things, for supernovae. It continues Zwicky's work with modern technology.
127237.m: The Zwicky Transient Facility continues Zwicky's search for supernovae.

127238.q: What did Michel Mayor and Didier Queloz achieve in 1995 at the Observatoire de Haute-Provence?
a: The discovery of the first planet orbiting a Sun-like star
The first image of a black hole
The first detection of gravitational waves
The discovery of the planet Neptune
127238.e: With the ELODIE spectrograph, developed in Geneva, they found a planet orbiting the star 51 Pegasi. For this they received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 2019.
127238.m: In 1995 the first planet orbiting a Sun-like star was discovered.

127239.q: Why does the radial velocity method used by Mayor give only a minimum mass for a planet on its own?
a: Because the tilt of the orbit relative to the line of sight is unknown
Because the star is too bright
Because planets do not give off light
Because the speed of light is too great
127239.e: Only the star's motion along the line of sight is measured. Without the orbital inclination you only know the product of the mass and the sine of the inclination angle.
127239.m: The radial velocity only reveals a minimum mass.

127240.q: A star is moving towards us at 60 m/s. Roughly how far does a spectral line at 500 nm shift (c equal to 3·10⁸ m/s)?
127240.e: For small speeds Δλ = λ · v / c = 500 nm · 60 / (3·10⁸) = 0.0001 nm. Measuring such tiny shifts was the great achievement of the Geneva group.
127240.m: Planets give themselves away through tiny line shifts.

127241.q: What does a spectrograph such as ESPRESSO at the Very Large Telescope measure to find planets?
a: Tiny shifts in a star's spectral lines
The temperature of the planet's surface
127241.e: A planet makes its star wobble slightly. Because of the Doppler effect the star's spectral lines shift back and forth very slightly. ESPRESSO continues the Geneva tradition of planet hunting.
127241.m: ESPRESSO continues the Geneva tradition of planet hunting.

127242.q: Which Basel mathematician is the University of Geneva's Swiss telescope at the La Silla Observatory in Chile named after?
127242.e: The University of Geneva's 1.2-metre telescope bears the name of the famous Basel mathematician Leonhard Euler. With it and the CORALIE spectrograph the Geneva team searched for many planets.
127242.m: A Swiss telescope in Chile bears the name Leonhard Euler.

127243.q: What distinguishes a brown dwarf from a true star?
a: No lasting hydrogen fusion takes place in it
It is made entirely of rock
It shines more brightly than the Sun
127243.e: Brown dwarfs are too light to fuse hydrogen permanently. From about 13 Jupiter masses a companion is no longer counted as a planet but as a brown dwarf.
127243.m: Brown dwarfs lie between planets and stars.

127244.q: Why does the Sun also move slightly back and forth, even though the planets orbit it?
a: The Sun and planets orbit a common centre of mass
The solar wind pushes the Sun
The Sun rotates about its own axis
The Milky Way tugs at it jerkily
127244.e: Jupiter in particular pulls so strongly that the common centre of mass lies just outside the Sun's surface. A distant observer would measure a wobble of the Sun of about 13 m/s.
127244.m: The Sun wobbles too, because of its planets.

127245.q: What does a radial velocity curve that is a pure sine curve reveal?
a: The planet moves on an almost circular orbit
The planet has a very eccentric orbit
127245.e: On a circular orbit the star's speed changes evenly, in a sine shape. Eccentric orbits, on the other hand, produce distorted, asymmetric curves.
127245.m: A pure sine curve points to a circular orbit.

127246.q: What did the Geneva astronomer Didier Queloz receive the Nobel Prize in Physics for in 2019, together with Michel Mayor?
a: For discovering a planet orbiting a Sun-like star
For the first image of a black hole
127246.e: In 1995 Mayor and Queloz discovered the planet 51 Pegasi b. It was the first exoplanet orbiting a Sun-like star.
127246.m: Queloz and Mayor found the first exoplanet orbiting a Sun-like star in 1995.

127247.q: In planet hunting, what does a redshift in a star's spectral lines reveal?
a: The star is moving away from us at that moment
127247.e: According to the Doppler effect, light waves are stretched when the source moves away. If redshift and blueshift alternate regularly, this points to a companion.
127247.m: Redshift means a star is moving away from us.

127248.q: Why does a star that has a planet itself move on a small orbit?
a: Both orbit their common centre of mass
The planet pushes the star away with solar wind
The star is pulled by the Milky Way's magnetic field
The star only moves because of its rotation
127248.e: Star and planet attract each other and orbit their common centre of mass. Because the star is much heavier, its orbit is very small.
127248.m: Star and planet orbit their common centre of mass.

127249.q: A planet has a radius one tenth of the star's radius. Roughly how much does the star's brightness drop during a transit?
127249.e: The dimming equals the area ratio (R_planet / R_star)² = (0.1)² = 0.01. Jupiter passing in front of the Sun would therefore dim it by about 1 %.
127249.m: The transit depth is the square of the ratio of the radii.

127250.q: Which property of an exoplanet can be calculated if you know its mass from the radial velocity and its radius from a transit?
127250.e: Mass and volume give the density. It shows whether a planet is made mostly of rock or mainly of gas.
127250.m: Mass and radius together reveal a planet's density.

127251.q: Why does a hot Jupiter such as 51 Pegasi b probably always show the same side to its star?
a: Because strong tidal forces have locked its rotation to its orbit
Because it does not rotate at all and does not orbit the star
Because its magnetic field holds it in place
Because it has a solid surface of ice
127251.e: Very close to the star, tidal forces slow down the planet's rotation until a rotation and an orbit take the same time. This is called tidal locking.
127251.m: Tidal forces can lock a planet's rotation to its orbit.

127252.q: How is it explained today that gas giants such as 51 Pegasi b are found so close to their star?
a: They formed further out and migrated inwards
They formed directly in the hot interior of the star
They were captured from other galaxies
127252.e: Close to the young star it is too hot to collect much gas and ice. But through interaction with the gas disc, planets can migrate inwards; this is called planetary migration.

127253.q: In planet hunting, what is meant by a star's radial velocity?
a: The part of its velocity along our line of sight
Its speed of rotation about its own axis
Its speed across the line of sight
The speed of its stellar wind
127253.e: Only motion towards us or away from us shifts the spectral lines. Motion across the line of sight remains invisible with this method.
127253.m: The radial velocity is the motion along the line of sight.

127254.q: In which city was the physicist and Nobel laureate Felix Bloch born in 1905?
127254.e: Felix Bloch was born in Zurich in 1905. He is one of the Swiss Nobel laureates in physics.

127255.q: What did Felix Bloch receive the Nobel Prize in Physics for in 1952, together with Edward Purcell?
a: For methods of measuring nuclear magnetic resonance
127255.e: Bloch and Purcell developed methods to measure the magnetic properties of atomic nuclei very precisely. This nuclear magnetic resonance is used today in chemistry and medicine.
127255.m: Bloch received the Nobel Prize for nuclear magnetic resonance.

127256.q: Which medical imaging method is based on nuclear magnetic resonance, which Felix Bloch helped to develop?
127256.e: MRI uses strong magnetic fields and radio waves to excite the nuclear spins of hydrogen atoms in the body. This produces detailed cross-sectional images without X-rays.
127256.m: Without nuclear magnetic resonance there would be no MRI.

127257.q: Which research organisation near Geneva did Felix Bloch lead in 1954 as its first Director-General?
127257.e: CERN was founded in 1954. Felix Bloch was its first Director-General but returned to Stanford University after only about a year.
127257.m: Felix Bloch was the first head of CERN.

127258.q: Under which famous physicist did Felix Bloch write his doctoral thesis in Leipzig?
127258.e: Bloch gained his doctorate in Leipzig in 1928 under Werner Heisenberg, one of the founders of quantum mechanics. In his thesis he described how electrons move in metals.
127258.m: Bloch was a doctoral student of Werner Heisenberg.

127259.q: What can be explained with the band model, to which Felix Bloch contributed with his work on electrons in crystals?
a: Why some substances conduct electricity and others do not
127259.e: Bloch showed how electrons behave in a regular crystal lattice. This led to the band model, which explains conductors, semiconductors and insulators.
127259.m: Bloch's work explains why metals conduct electricity.

127260.q: At which university did Felix Bloch begin his studies before moving to Leipzig?
127260.e: Bloch first studied at ETH Zurich, where he switched from engineering to physics. There he attended lectures by Erwin Schrödinger, among others.
127260.m: Felix Bloch studied at ETH Zurich.

127261.q: Why did Felix Bloch leave Germany in 1933?
a: Because the Nazis came to power and he was of Jewish origin
Because he wanted to become a Federal Councillor in Switzerland
Because his university was closed to build a stadium
Because he received an offer to work as a musician
127261.e: After the Nazis took power, many Jewish scientists lost their posts. Bloch emigrated to the USA soon afterwards.
127261.m: Like many researchers, Bloch had to leave Germany in 1933.

127262.q: Which element did chemists in Berlin detect in 1938 after bombarding uranium with neutrons?
127262.e: Barium is much lighter than uranium, which was puzzling at first. Lise Meitner provided the physical explanation.
127262.m: Detecting barium was the key to a great discovery.

127263.q: Which famous physicist's lectures did Lise Meitner attend while studying in Vienna?
127263.e: Boltzmann inspired Meitner's enthusiasm for theoretical physics. In 1906 she became one of the first women to gain a doctorate in physics at the University of Vienna.
127263.m: Ludwig Boltzmann shaped the young Lise Meitner.

127264.q: Which physicist did Lise Meitner become assistant to in Berlin, as one of the first women in Prussia in such a post?
127264.e: Meitner came to Berlin in 1907 to attend Planck's lectures. Later she became his assistant, which was rare for a woman at the time.
127264.m: Lise Meitner worked as Max Planck's assistant.

127266.q: With which model of the atomic nucleus did Meitner and Frisch explain why a uranium nucleus can break apart?
127266.e: They imagined the nucleus as a charged drop of liquid. If it absorbs a neutron, it can deform and split into two parts.
127266.m: The liquid drop model explains why heavy nuclei can split.

127267.q: Who received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry for the discovery of nuclear fission, without Lise Meitner being honoured too?
127267.e: Otto Hahn received the 1944 Nobel Prize in Chemistry, awarded in 1945. Lise Meitner, who explained nuclear fission in terms of physics, went away empty-handed.
127267.m: Otto Hahn received the Nobel Prize for nuclear fission alone.

127268.q: Which sentence is on Lise Meitner's gravestone in England?
a: “A physicist who never lost her humanity”
127268.e: Her nephew Otto Robert Frisch chose the English inscription “A physicist who never lost her humanity”. It honours Meitner's attitude, such as her refusal to take part in military research.
127268.m: Lise Meitner's gravestone honours her humanity.

127271.q: What is the Max Planck Society?
a: An organisation for basic research in Germany
127271.e: The Max Planck Society was founded in 1948. It runs many research institutes in Germany, mainly for basic research.
127271.m: The Max Planck Society supports basic research.

127272.q: What does the Planck constant h, named after Max Planck, describe?
a: The relationship between the energy and frequency of a light quantum
The speed of light in a vacuum
127272.e: For a light quantum, E = h · f. The higher the frequency of the light, the more energy a single quantum carries.
127272.m: A light quantum has the energy h times f.

127273.q: Why is the Planck length special in physics?
a: Below it, today's physical theories break down
It is exactly the diameter of an atom
It is the length of the original metre bar in Paris
It is the wavelength of visible light
127273.e: The Planck length is about 10²⁰ times smaller than a proton. For such small distances you would need a theory that unites quantum physics and gravity.
127273.m: The Planck length is unimaginably small.

a: The time light takes to travel one Planck length
The lifetime of a free neutron
The length of one oscillation of visible light
127274.e: At about 5·10⁻⁴⁴ seconds the Planck time is unimaginably short. For even shorter times today's physical theories break down.
127274.m: The Planck time is the shortest meaningful time span in today's physics.

127275.q: According to Wien's displacement law, at which wavelength does the Sun (about 5800 K) radiate most strongly (b equal to 2.9·10⁻³ m·K)?
127275.e: λ_max = b / T = 2.9·10⁻³ m·K / 5800 K = 5·10⁻⁷ m = 500 nm. This law follows from Planck's radiation law.
127275.m: Hotter bodies radiate most strongly at shorter wavelengths.

127276.q: Which famous physicist received the first Max Planck Medal in 1929 together with Planck himself?
127276.e: The Max Planck Medal is the German Physical Society's highest award for theoretical physics. At the first award in 1929, medals went to Planck and Einstein.
127276.m: Planck and Einstein were the first to receive the Max Planck Medal.

127277.q: What advice is the young Max Planck said to have received from his professor Philipp von Jolly?
a: Not to study physics, as almost everything there had been discovered
To emigrate to America at once
To study medicine rather than mathematics
127277.e: Jolly thought there were only a few gaps left to fill in physics. Yet it was Planck who later started a revolution with quantum theory.
127277.m: Planck studied physics despite the warning that there was nothing new to discover.

127278.q: Which area of physics did Max Planck deal with in his doctoral thesis?
127278.e: Planck wrote about the second law of thermodynamics. His interest in entropy later led him to black-body radiation.
127278.m: Planck's path to quantum theory began in thermodynamics.

127571.q: What do people do in bionics?
a: Count the stars in the sky
127571.e: In bionics, researchers look closely at how animals and plants solve problems. Then they use these ideas for new technology.

127573.q: Which plant was the model for Velcro?
127573.e: Burdock burrs easily get caught on clothes and fur. Velcro holds in exactly the same way.
127573.m: Velcro was copied from the burdock.

127574.q: Which country did the inventor of Velcro come from?
127574.e: The engineer George de Mestral came from the canton of Vaud. He had his invention protected in the middle of the 20th century.
127574.m: Velcro was invented by a Swiss man.

127575.q: Where did the inventor of Velcro discover lots of burrs?
127575.e: After a walk, lots of burrs were stuck in his dog's fur. He looked at them closely under the microscope.
127575.m: A walk with the dog gave him the idea for Velcro.

127576.q: What does a burr have on its spines?
127576.e: The spines of the burr end in little hooks. With them, they catch in fur or fabric.
127576.m: A burr holds on with tiny hooks.

127577.q: What does the second side of a Velcro fastener have, which the hooks catch in?
127577.e: One side of the Velcro has hooks, the other lots of soft loops. If you press them together, they catch on each other.
127577.m: Hooks and loops hold Velcro together.

127578.q: What does a bionics expert do first?
127578.e: First you have to understand how an animal or plant does something. Only then can you turn the idea into technology.
127578.m: People who work in bionics observe nature first.

127579.q: What does water do on a lotus leaf?
127579.e: The lotus leaf is water-repellent. Drops of water simply roll over it.
127579.m: Water rolls off a lotus leaf in beads.

127580.q: What do the rolling water drops take with them from the lotus leaf?
127580.e: The rolling drops collect dust and dirt and carry them away. This makes the leaf clean.
127580.m: Water drops wash the lotus leaf clean.

127581.q: What is it called when a leaf keeps itself clean?
127581.e: With the lotus, rain is enough to make the leaf clean again. This is called self-cleaning.
127581.m: The lotus leaf can clean itself.

127582.q: What does the surface of a lotus leaf have when you magnify it a lot?
127582.e: Under the microscope you can see lots of tiny bumps. Drops only touch them in a few places.
127582.m: Tiny bumps make the lotus leaf water-repellent.

127583.q: What else is the lotus leaf covered with?
127583.e: A fine layer of wax repels water. Together with the bumps, this creates the lotus effect.
127583.m: Fine wax helps the lotus leaf repel water.

127584.q: Where does the lotus plant grow?
127584.e: The lotus is a water plant and grows in ponds and lakes. Its large leaves lie on the water or stick up above it.
127584.m: The lotus is a water plant.

127585.q: Which product uses the lotus effect?
127585.e: There are outdoor wall paints with a surface like a lotus leaf. Rain washes the dirt off the wall of the house.
127585.m: Some house paints stay clean thanks to the lotus effect.

127586.q: What colour is the flower of the lotus plant often?
127586.e: The large flowers of the lotus are often pink, sometimes white too. They stick up high above the water.
127586.m: The lotus often has large pink flowers.

127587.q: What shape is a water drop on a lotus leaf?
127587.e: Because the leaf repels the water, the drop pulls together almost into a ball. That way it can roll off easily.
127587.m: On a lotus leaf, drops become almost perfectly round.

127588.q: What does shark skin feel like when you stroke it from the tail to the head?
127588.e: A shark's skin is covered in tiny hard scales. That is why it feels rough when you stroke it the wrong way.
127588.m: Stroked the wrong way, shark skin is rough.

127589.q: What is the surface of shark skin made of?
127589.e: A shark's scales look like little teeth. That is why they are called skin teeth.
127589.m: A shark has tiny teeth on its skin.

127590.q: What do the fine grooves on shark skin help with?
a: Gliding through the water more easily
127590.e: The grooves on the skin teeth guide the water and reduce drag. So the shark swims using less strength.
127590.m: Shark skin helps the shark glide easily through the water.

127591.q: Which sportswear was made with shark skin as a model?
127591.e: Swimsuits with a surface like shark skin were meant to reduce drag in the water. The idea was to swim faster.
127591.m: There were swimsuits modelled on shark skin.

127592.q: What is a ship's paint modelled on shark skin meant to prevent?
a: Mussels and algae growing on it
127592.e: Hardly any algae or mussels settle on the skin of sharks. People want to achieve that for ships too.
127592.m: Shark skin stays free of mussels and algae.

127593.q: Which vehicles are given a film like shark skin to save fuel?
127593.e: A film with tiny grooves reduces air resistance. So aeroplanes need slightly less fuel.
127593.m: Shark-skin film helps aeroplanes save fuel.

127594.q: Which animal group do sharks belong to?
127594.e: Sharks breathe with gills and spend their whole life in water. They are fish.

127595.q: Where can a gecko even walk?
127595.e: Geckos cling so well that they can walk upside down on the ceiling. Even smooth panes of glass are no problem for them.
127595.m: A gecko can walk upside down on the ceiling.

127596.q: What does a gecko have on the underside of its toes?
127596.e: On the toes there are millions of tiny hairs. They get so close to the wall that they stick to it.
127596.m: Fine hairs let the gecko stick to walls.

127597.q: What does a gecko NOT need to stick to a pane of glass?
127597.e: The gecko sticks without any glue. It is only the tiny hairs on its toes that hold it on.
127597.m: A gecko sticks without any glue.

127598.q: Which animal group does the gecko belong to?
127598.e: Geckos are lizards and so they are reptiles. They have scaly skin.

127599.q: What have researchers developed with the gecko as a model?
a: Sticky tape that can be removed again
Glasses that see in the dark
127599.e: Modelled on gecko toes, there are sticky strips without glue. You can remove them and use them again.
127599.m: Gecko tape sticks and can be removed again.

127600.q: When are many geckos out and about?
127600.e: Many types of gecko hunt insects at night. During the day they hide.
127600.m: Many geckos are active at night.

127601.q: How does a gecko get its foot off the wall again?
127601.e: The gecko peels its toes off from the tip like sticky tape. That way it frees its foot very easily.
127601.m: A gecko peels off its toes to let go.

127602.q: What can a gecko shed when in danger?
127602.e: If an enemy grabs the gecko by the tail, it sheds it and escapes. The tail then grows back.
127602.m: A gecko can shed its tail.

127603.q: What does a spider build its web from?
127603.e: The spider makes its threads itself. The material is called spider silk.
127603.m: Spider webs are made of spider silk.

127604.q: Where on the spider are the threads made?
a: On the back part of the body
127604.e: At the end of the back part of its body, the spider has spinnerets. The silk comes out there.
127604.m: The spider spins its threads at the back of its body.

127605.q: A spider's thread is very thin. Does that make it weak?
127605.e: Spider silk is amazingly strong. For its thickness, it can take more than a steel wire of the same thinness.
127605.m: Spider silk is thin but very strong.

127606.q: What can a spider's thread do especially well without breaking?
127606.e: Spider silk is very stretchy. So the web catches a flying insect without tearing.
127606.m: Spider threads are stretchy and do not break easily.

127607.q: What is spider silk made of?
127607.e: Spider silk is made of proteins. Researchers are trying to produce these proteins artificially.
127607.m: Spider silk is made of protein.

127608.q: What would people like to use artificial spider silk for, for example?
127608.e: Spider silk is strong and the body accepts it well. So it could be used in medicine, for example for stitches.
127608.m: Artificial spider silk could help in medicine.

127609.q: Why doesn't a spider get stuck in its own web?
a: It walks on threads that are not sticky
It washes the web with water
127609.e: Not all the threads in the web are sticky. The spider walks mainly on the dry threads.
127609.m: The spider knows the dry threads in its web.

127610.q: What does a spider catch with its web?
127610.e: Flies, mosquitoes and other insects get caught in the web. The spider then eats them.
127610.m: Spiders catch insects in their webs.

127611.e: Many types of termite build large mounds. A whole colony lives inside.

127612.q: What do termites build their mounds from?
127612.e: Termites mix soil with their saliva. When the mixture dries, it becomes rock hard.
127612.m: Termite mounds are built from soil and saliva.

127613.q: What provides fresh air in a termite mound?
127613.e: Air flows through the mound through many tunnels and shafts. This keeps it pleasant inside.
127613.m: Tunnels and channels air the termite mound.

127614.q: On which continent is there a well-known office building that is aired like a termite mound?
127614.e: In Zimbabwe, a large building was built that airs itself on the model of termite mounds. That is why it needs much less energy for ventilation and cooling.
127614.m: A building in Africa airs itself like a termite mound.

127615.q: What does a building designed like a termite mound save?
127615.e: The air is cooled without big machines. That is why the building needs much less electricity.

127616.e: Termites like warmth. Most kinds live in the tropics and other warm areas.
127616.m: Termites live mainly in warm countries.

127617.q: How high can termite mounds get?
127617.e: Some termite mounds are taller than an adult. They can be several metres high.
127617.m: Termite mounds can be several metres high.

127618.e: Many termites eat wood and other plant parts. That is why they can also damage wooden houses.

127619.e: The boxfish has an angular body. It looks like a little box.
127619.m: The boxfish is square like a box.

127620.q: What surrounds the body of the boxfish?
127620.e: The boxfish lives inside a shell of bony plates. Only its fins, eyes and mouth stick out.
127620.m: The boxfish wears a hard shell.

127621.q: What was built with the boxfish as a model?
127621.e: A car maker built a test car in the shape of the boxfish. It was meant to have little air resistance.
127621.m: A car was modelled on the boxfish.

127622.q: What does the boxfish mainly swim with?
a: Its whole body like a snake
A jet of water like a squid
127622.e: The hard shell can hardly bend. That is why the boxfish moves mainly with its small fins.
127622.m: The boxfish swims with its fins.

a: In the sea near coral reefs
127623.e: Boxfish live in warm seas. They are often found near coral reefs.
127623.m: The boxfish lives in the sea near corals.

127624.q: What does the young yellow boxfish look like?
127624.e: The young yellow boxfish is bright yellow and has black spots. The colour warns enemies.
127624.m: The young yellow boxfish is yellow with black spots.

127625.q: What can the boxfish release when in danger?
127625.e: The boxfish can release poison through its skin. This protects it from enemies.
127625.m: The boxfish protects itself with poison.

127626.q: What did engineers learn from the boxfish's shell?
a: How to build light but strong
How to build as heavy as possible
How to build only with glass
How to build only round parts
127626.e: The boxfish's shell is light and yet very strong. This is also useful for cars and machines.
127626.m: The boxfish shows how to build light and strong.

127627.q: Which vehicle was given a nose modelled on the kingfisher's beak?
127627.e: Engineers in Japan shaped the front of a high-speed train like a kingfisher's beak. The kingfisher was a good model for this.
127627.m: A Japanese high-speed train has a nose like a kingfisher.

127628.q: What problem did the high-speed train in Japan used to have when leaving a tunnel?
127628.e: The train pushed the air in the tunnel along in front of it. When it came out, there was a loud bang.
127628.m: The new train nose helped against the bang at the tunnel.

127629.q: How does the kingfisher dive into the water?
127629.e: The kingfisher's beak is shaped so that it slides into the water with almost no splash. That is why it was a good model.
127629.m: The kingfisher dives in with almost no splash.

127630.q: What does the kingfisher mainly eat?
127630.e: The kingfisher sits on a branch over the water. When it sees a small fish, it plunges in.

127631.q: What colour is the kingfisher's back?
127631.e: The kingfisher has a bright blue back and an orange breast. It is one of the most colourful birds in Switzerland.
127631.m: The kingfisher has a bright blue back.

127632.q: Where can you watch kingfishers in Switzerland?
127632.e: The kingfisher needs clear water with small fish. That is why it lives by water.
127632.m: You find the kingfisher by water.

127633.q: What did the high-speed train with the kingfisher nose need less of than before?
127633.e: With the new nose, the train has to push away less air. That is why it uses less electricity.
127633.m: The kingfisher nose saves the train electricity.

127634.q: Where does the kingfisher make its nest?
a: In a tunnel in an earth bank
127634.e: The kingfisher digs a tunnel into a steep earth bank by the water. The nest is at the end of the tunnel.
127634.m: The kingfisher nests in a tunnel in the riverbank.

127635.q: What does the humpback whale have on the front edge of its flippers?
127635.e: The front edge of the flipper is not smooth but has lots of bumps. It looks like a row of lumps.
127635.m: The humpback whale's flipper has bumps.

127636.q: What do the bumps on its flippers help the humpback whale to do?
127636.e: The bumps guide the water well around the flipper. So the big whale can swim in surprisingly tight turns.
127636.m: Thanks to the bumps, the humpback whale is very agile.

127637.q: Which machines were given blades with bumps modelled on the humpback whale?
127637.e: Rotor blades with bumps like the humpback whale's are meant to use the wind better. Fans have also been built this way.
127637.m: Some wind turbines have bumps like the humpback whale.

127638.q: What is special about the humpback whale's flippers?
127638.e: The humpback whale has the longest flippers of all whales. They are about a third as long as its body.
127638.m: The humpback whale has very long flippers.

127639.q: Which animal group does the humpback whale belong to?
127639.e: Whales breathe with lungs and feed their young with milk. That is why they are mammals, even though they live in the sea.
127639.m: The humpback whale is a mammal.

127640.q: What are humpback whales famous for?
127640.e: Male humpback whales sing long songs made of many sounds. They can be heard far away underwater.

127641.q: What does the humpback whale eat?
127641.e: The humpback whale has no teeth, but baleen plates. With them, it sieves krill and small fish out of the water.
127641.m: The humpback whale eats krill and small fish.

127642.q: How does the humpback whale drive fish together into a shoal?
a: With a net of air bubbles
127642.e: The humpback whale swims in a circle and blows out air bubbles. The fish stay trapped in this bubble net.
127642.m: Humpback whales hunt with a net of air bubbles.

127643.q: What does a streamlined shape look like?
a: Round at the front and narrow at the back
Flat at the front and wide at the back
127643.e: A body that is round at the front and gets narrower towards the back glides well through air and water. This shape is called streamlined.
127643.m: A streamlined shape is round at the front and narrow at the back.

127644.q: Which bird swims very fast underwater thanks to its streamlined shape?
127644.e: The penguin has a smooth, spindle-shaped body. With it, it shoots through the water like a torpedo.
127644.m: The penguin is a fast swimmer.

127645.q: Why are vehicles often built with a streamlined shape?
127645.e: A streamlined shape is slowed down less by the air. That is why a vehicle needs less fuel or electricity.

127646.q: Which shape is thought to be especially good for gliding through the air?
127646.e: A falling drop is round at the front and pointed at the back. This shape gives the air very little resistance.
127646.m: The teardrop shape glides well through the air.

127647.q: What slows you down when you ride your bike fast, even when there is no wind?
a: The air you have to push away
127647.e: When you ride, the bike has to push the air aside. The faster you go, the more this air slows you down. This is called air resistance.
127647.m: Air resistance slows you down when cycling.

127648.q: Why do racing cyclists crouch low over the handlebars?
a: So less air slows them down
So they can see the road better
So the saddle is more comfortable
127648.e: If you crouch down, you give the air a smaller surface. That way the headwind slows you down less.
127648.m: Crouching makes you faster because less air slows you down.

127649.q: Which fish is a fast swimmer with a streamlined shape?
127649.e: The tuna has a spindle-shaped body like a torpedo. It is one of the fastest fish.
127649.m: Thanks to its shape, the tuna is a fast swimmer.

127650.q: Where do people test how much a car is slowed down by the wind?
127650.e: In a wind tunnel, a strong wind blows at the car. This shows how the air flows past it.
127650.m: Air resistance is tested in a wind tunnel.

127651.q: Which famous artist drew flying machines modelled on birds more than 500 years ago?
127651.e: Leonardo da Vinci watched birds closely and drew flying machines. But they could not fly yet.
127651.m: Leonardo da Vinci dreamed of flying like a bird.

127652.q: Which bird did the flight pioneer Otto Lilienthal study especially closely?
127652.e: Otto Lilienthal studied how storks fly. Then he built flying machines and flew them himself.
127652.m: Otto Lilienthal learned from the stork.

127653.q: How is a bird’s wing shaped, much like an aeroplane wing?
127653.e: The wing is curved on top. When air flows over it, an upward force called lift is created.
127653.m: A curved wing lifts birds and aeroplanes into the air.

127654.q: What do many aeroplanes have at their wingtips, copied from birds?
127654.e: Birds of prey spread the feathers at the ends of their wings and bend them upwards. Bent wingtips on aeroplanes also save fuel.
127654.m: Aeroplanes copied bent wingtips from birds.

127655.q: Which bird flies almost silently and was the model for quiet fans?
127655.e: An owl’s feathers have fine fringes along the edge. That is why you can hardly hear it fly, and fans built this way are quieter too.

127656.q: Why do migrating birds such as geese often fly in a V shape?
127656.e: Each bird uses the rising air from the bird in front of it. That way they all save energy on the long journey.
127656.m: Flying in a V shape saves migrating birds energy.

127657.q: What makes many bird bones especially light?
127657.e: Many bird bones are hollow inside and supported by thin struts. This makes them light but still strong.

127658.q: What is it called when a bird floats through the air without flapping its wings?
127658.e: When gliding, the bird keeps its wings still and slowly floats downwards. This saves energy.
127658.m: When gliding, a bird does not flap its wings.

127659.q: What does a cone do when the weather is dry?
127659.e: In dry air the scales spread apart. In damp weather they close again.
127659.m: A cone opens when it is dry.

127660.q: Why does a cone open in dry weather?
a: So the seeds can fly away
So birds can live in it
127660.e: The seeds have little wings. In dry weather the wind carries them far away.
127660.m: The cone opens so the wind can spread the seeds.

127661.q: What does a cone need to open and close?
127661.e: A cone still moves even when it fell from the tree a long time ago. It does not need muscles for this, only dry or damp air.

127662.q: Why do the scales of a cone bend?
a: Two layers swell by different amounts
127662.e: Each scale has two layers. When it is damp, one layer expands more than the other, so the scale bends.
127662.m: Two different layers make the scale bend.

127663.q: Which idea for clothing was copied from cones?
a: Fabric that opens air holes when you sweat
Fabric that glows in the dark
127663.e: Like the scales of a cone, tiny flaps in the fabric can open when it gets damp. This lets more air reach the skin.
127663.m: Clothing modelled on cones airs itself.

127664.q: Where are the seeds in a cone?
127664.e: The seeds lie protected under each scale. They can only get out once the scale opens.
127664.m: The seeds lie under the scales of the cone.

127665.q: How do the cones of the silver fir sit on the branch?
127665.e: The cones of the silver fir stand upright on the branches. They fall apart up there and do not drop down whole.
127665.m: Fir cones stand upright on the branch.

127666.q: Which tree do most of the cones you find on the ground in a Swiss forest come from?
127666.e: Spruce cones hang down and fall to the ground whole. Even so, many people call them “fir cones”.
127666.m: The cones on the forest floor are usually spruce cones.

127667.q: Which animal likes to get the seeds out of cones?
127667.e: The squirrel gnaws off the scales and eats the seeds. What is left is a gnawed core.
127667.m: Squirrels eat the seeds from cones.

127668.q: Where is the water pressure in a lake greatest?
a: Right at the top at the surface
127668.e: The deeper you dive, the more water there is above you. This water pushes down with its weight.
127668.m: The deeper the water, the greater the pressure.

127669.q: A cup has a hole near the top and a hole near the bottom on its side. From which hole does the water spray further?
127669.e: There is more water above the bottom hole, so the pressure there is greater. The water is pushed out more strongly.
127669.m: At the bottom of the cup, the water pushes harder than at the top.

127670.q: A house has a tap on the ground floor and one on the top floor. Where does the water usually come out with more pressure?
127670.e: The water on the ground floor has more water in the pipe above it. So it pushes harder there than at the very top.
127670.m: Water pressure is greater at the bottom of a house than at the top.

127671.q: Where does the pressure in the water of a swimming pool come from?
127671.e: Water is heavy. The water higher up pushes on the water further down.
127671.m: The weight of the water creates water pressure.

127672.q: From which side does water push on a diver?
127672.e: Water pushes in all directions at once. That is why a diver feels the pressure all around.

127673.q: A full water bag has a small hole. What happens if you squeeze the bag hard?
a: The water squirts out more strongly
127673.e: When you squeeze, the pressure in the bag gets bigger. The water is pushed through the hole faster.
127673.m: More pressure makes the water squirt harder.

127674.q: Why do submarines have very thick, strong walls?
a: So the water pressure doesn't crush them
127674.e: In the deep, a huge amount of water presses on the submarine. Strong walls can withstand this pressure.
127674.m: Deep in the sea, a submarine needs very strong walls.

127675.q: What can you use to measure the pressure in a water pipe?
127675.e: A pressure gauge shows how hard the water in the pipe is pushing. A thermometer, on the other hand, measures warmth.
127675.m: Water pressure is measured with a pressure gauge.

127676.q: What happens to an empty plastic bottle with the lid screwed on if you push it deep into water?
127676.e: In the deep, the water pushes hard on the outside of the bottle. The air inside is squeezed and the bottle gets dents.

127677.q: What is the famous big fountain in Geneva called?
127677.e: The Jet d'eau stands in Lake Geneva and is a landmark of Geneva. The name is French and means ‘water jet’.
127677.m: The Jet d'eau is the landmark of Geneva.

127678.q: Roughly how high does the Jet d'eau in Geneva spray?
127678.e: Powerful pumps push the water about 140 metres into the air. That is higher than most church towers.
127678.m: The Jet d'eau sprays higher than a church tower.

127679.q: What does a modern fountain need to make the water spray up?
127679.e: The pump pushes the water up through the nozzle with force. Without a pump, the water would just lie there.
127679.m: A pump makes the water in a fountain spray up.

127680.q: In many fountains, where does the water that keeps spraying up come from?
a: It is collected in the basin and pumped up again
It comes fresh from the sea each time
It is made in the nozzle
127680.e: Many fountains use the same water again and again. It falls into the basin and the pump pushes it up once more.
127680.m: Many fountains pump their water round in a circle.

127681.q: Why does the water of a fountain fall back down?
127681.e: The Earth pulls everything downwards, including water. That is why the jet falls back into the basin after going up.
127681.m: Gravity pulls the water back down.

127682.q: In the past, fountains had no motor pump. What did they use instead?
127682.e: If the water comes down a pipe from higher up, it pushes downwards. At the lower fountain it then sprays up and out.
127682.m: Water from higher up can power a fountain without a pump.

127683.q: A fountain without a pump gets its water from a spring on a hillside. How high can its jet spray at most?
a: Almost as high as the spring
Twice as high as the spring
127683.e: Water cannot rise higher than where it comes from. Because it is slowed down on the way, the jet even stays a little lower.
127683.m: Without a pump, water never rises higher than its source.

127684.q: What can you often see in the fine spray of a fountain when the sun is shining?
127684.e: The sun shines through the many little water droplets. The droplets split the light into its colours.
127684.m: Sun and water droplets make a rainbow.

127685.q: What is a water tower for?
127685.e: The tank at the top of the tower holds a large supply of water. From there the water flows into the houses.
127685.m: A water tower stores water high up.

127686.q: Why is the tank of a water tower so high up?
a: So the water flows into the houses with pressure
So it can be seen better
127686.e: Water flows from top to bottom. The higher the tank, the harder the water pushes in the pipes.
127686.m: Water stored high up gives pressure in the pipes.

127687.q: What brings the water from the water tower into the pipes of the houses?
127687.e: The water flows downwards by itself because the Earth pulls it. This way it gets through the pipes to the tap.
127687.m: With a water tower, gravity does the work.

127688.q: How does the water get into the tank at the top of the water tower?
a: It is carried up in buckets
It only falls in as rain
It is lifted with a crane
127688.e: Pumps push the water up through a pipe. This often happens at night, when little water is needed.
127688.m: Pumps fill the water tower from below.

127689.q: A house stands higher than the tank of the water tower. Without an extra pump, what happens on the top floor?
a: The water sprays out very strongly
127689.e: Water does not flow by itself higher than its tank. That is why such a high house needs its own pump.
127689.m: Water does not rise higher than its tank.

127690.q: What is a large water store called that in Switzerland is often in the ground on a hill?
127690.e: Instead of towers, Switzerland often builds reservoirs into hills. Because they are high up, they work like a water tower.
127690.m: A reservoir on a hill works like a water tower.

127691.q: When is a water tower especially useful?
a: When lots of people need water at the same time
127691.e: In the morning many people shower at the same time. Then the supply in the tower delivers enough water quickly.
127691.m: The supply in a water tower helps when everyone needs water at once.

127692.q: What happens to the water pressure in the houses when the tank in the water tower is almost empty?
127692.e: The pressure depends on how high the water stands in the tower. If the water level falls, the water pushes less hard.
127692.m: A full water tower gives more pressure than an empty one.

127693.q: Two glasses are connected at the bottom by a tube. You pour water into one glass. What happens?
a: The water stands at the same height in both glasses
It all stays in the first glass
It stands higher in the second glass
127693.e: The water flows across through the tube. It keeps flowing until it is at the same height in both glasses.
127693.m: In connected containers, water stands at the same height.

127694.q: What are containers called that are connected to each other at the bottom?
127694.e: ‘Communicating’ here means ‘connected to each other’. The water can flow back and forth between the vessels.
127694.m: Containers connected at the bottom are called communicating vessels.

127695.q: Which part under the washbasin works like communicating vessels?
127695.e: A little water always stays in the curved pipe. This water keeps bad smells from the drain out.
127695.m: The trap holds back smells with water.

127696.q: A wide glass and a narrow glass are connected at the bottom. Where does the water stand higher?
a: At the same height in both
In the glass that is closer
127696.e: The shape of the containers does not matter. In connected containers, water always stands at the same height.
127696.m: The shape of the containers does not change the water level.

127697.q: Builders fill a long, see-through hose with water to mark two points at the same height. What is this tool called?
127697.e: The water stands at the same height at both ends. This way you can find the same height even on walls far apart.
127697.m: With a hose level you can find the same height in two places.

127698.q: Two glasses are connected at the bottom. What happens if you lift one glass up?
a: Water flows into the lower glass
The water stays where it is
Water flows into the raised glass
127698.e: The water wants to stand at the same height in both glasses. So it flows down into the lower glass.
127698.m: Water flows until it is at the same height everywhere.

127699.q: A kettle has a see-through tube on its side that is connected to the kettle at the bottom. Why can you see in it how much water is in the kettle?
a: The water in the tube stands as high as in the kettle
There is a tiny camera in the tube
The tube lights up when there is water
127699.e: The kettle and the tube are connected at the bottom. So the water in both is at the same height.
127699.m: A connected tube shows the water level.

127700.q: A U-shaped tube is half full of water. You blow into one end. What happens?
a: The water rises on the other side
The water rises on your side
127700.e: Your breath pushes the water down on your side. In return, it rises on the other side.
127700.m: If you push on one side, the water rises on the other.

a: Raising or lowering boats to a different water level
127701.e: Some rivers have steps, for example at a power station. The lock raises or lowers the boat so it can carry on.
127701.m: A lock is a lift for boats.

127702.q: What is the part of a lock called where the boat waits?
127702.e: The lock chamber is a long basin with gates at both ends. The water level is changed inside it.
127702.m: In the lock chamber, the boat is raised or lowered.

127703.q: A boat wants to go up in the lock. What happens in the lock chamber?
a: The boat is lifted by a crane
127703.e: When water flows into the chamber, the water level rises. The boat floats on top and is lifted with it.
127703.m: More water in the chamber lifts the boat.

127704.q: What closes off the lock chamber at the front and back?
127704.e: Large, watertight gates hold the water in the chamber. They only open when the boat may carry on.
127704.m: Strong gates hold the water in the lock.

127705.q: A boat wants to go down in the lock. What happens to the water in the chamber?
127705.e: When water flows out of the chamber, the water level falls. The boat slowly sinks down with it.
127705.m: Less water in the chamber lowers the boat.

127706.q: Does a lock need a pump to fill the chamber?
a: No, the water flows in from the higher side
Yes, the boat pumps it itself
No, it is filled with buckets
127706.e: You open sluices to the higher side. The water flows in by itself until it is at the same height.
127706.m: A lock fills itself with water from above.

127707.q: Why is a lock gate only opened when the water is at the same height on both sides?
a: Otherwise the water pushes too hard against the gate
Otherwise the boat gets too light
127707.e: If the water is higher on one side, it pushes against the gate with great force. Only when the heights are equal can it be opened easily.
127707.m: A lock gate is only opened when the water is level.

127708.q: Large cargo ships travel as far as Basel and pass through locks on the way. Which river do they travel on?
127708.e: The Rhine is an important waterway from the North Sea to Basel. At the power stations, locks lift the ships.
127708.m: Large ships travel on the Rhine as far as Basel.

127709.q: What happens if you partly cover the end of the garden hose with your thumb?
127709.e: The water has to go through a smaller opening. It gets faster and flies further.
127709.m: A small opening makes the jet of water faster.

127710.q: What happens if someone stands on the garden hose?
127710.e: The foot squashes the hose. So less water can flow through.
127710.m: A squashed hose lets less water through.

127711.q: A garden hose has been lying in the sun for a long time. What do you notice when you turn it on?
127711.e: The sun warms the hose and the water inside it. Only after that does cool water come from the pipe.
127711.m: The sun warms the water in the hose.

127712.q: A spray nozzle has lots of small holes. How does the water come out?
127712.e: The water is spread out over lots of small holes. This creates many fine jets, like rain.
127712.m: Lots of small holes make a gentle spray.

127713.q: A garden hose full of water is not connected. You lift one end. Which way does the water flow?
127713.e: Water always flows downwards. So it runs out of the hose at the low end.

127714.q: What is the frame on wheels called that you roll a long garden hose onto?
127714.e: The hose is wound onto the hose reel cart. This way it doesn't get tangled and is easy to pull around.
127714.m: A hose reel cart keeps the garden hose tidy.

127715.q: A loose garden hose sprays hard and wriggles back and forth. Why?
a: The water shooting out pushes the hose back
127715.e: When water shoots forwards quickly, the hose is pushed backwards. This push is called recoil.
127715.m: The recoil of the water moves the hose.

127716.q: With a hose full of water you can empty a paddling pool over its edge. Where must the outer end be?
a: Lower than the water in the pool
Higher than the edge of the pool
In the middle of the pool
127716.e: This is how a siphon works. If the outer end is lower, the water flows over the edge by itself.
127716.m: A siphon only works if the end is lower.

127717.q: Why should you empty the garden hose before winter?
a: Freezing water expands and can break it
Otherwise it turns blue in winter
127717.e: Ice takes up more space than water. When the water in the hose freezes, it can split the hose.
127717.m: Ice takes up more space than water.

127718.q: What happens in a simple water pistol when you pull the trigger?
a: A small pump pushes water out
127718.e: With the trigger you move a small pump. It pushes the water from the tank through the nozzle.
127718.m: In a water pistol, a small pump pushes the water out.

127719.q: Why should you never aim a water pistol at other people's eyes?
a: The jet can hurt the eyes
127719.e: A fast jet of water hits with force. The eyes are delicate and can be hurt.
127719.m: Never aim a water pistol at the eyes.

127720.q: With big water pistols you pump several times before spraying. What gets squeezed together?
127720.e: As you pump, more and more air goes into the tank. The squeezed air then pushes the water out.
127720.m: Squeezed air pushes the water out of the tank.

127721.q: What happens to the jet of a pumped-up water pistol if you spray for a long time?
127721.e: With every squirt, the air in the tank has more room. So it pushes less hard and the jet gets shorter.
127721.m: Over time, the pressure in the water pistol drops.

127722.q: You squirt a water pistol straight ahead. What path does the jet of water take?
a: It stays still in the air
127722.e: Gravity pulls the water downwards during its flight. That is why the jet makes a curve.
127722.m: A jet of water always flies in a curve.

127723.q: How should you aim so that the jet of a water pistol flies as far as possible?
127723.e: If you aim upwards at an angle, the water stays in the air longer and flies further. Straight up, it just falls back.
127723.m: Aimed upwards at an angle, the jet flies furthest.

127724.q: How does the jet of a simple water pistol get stronger?
a: If you squeeze faster and harder
127724.e: If you squeeze faster, you push the water through the nozzle faster. Then the jet flies further.
127724.m: Squeezing fast gives a strong jet.

127725.q: The tank of a pump-up water pistol has a hole. What happens when you pump?
a: The air escapes and the jet stays weak
127725.e: The air can get out again through the hole. So no pressure builds up in the tank to push the water out hard.
127725.m: A leaky tank cannot hold pressure.

127726.q: What do you need a watering can for?
127726.e: With a watering can you carry water to the plants. Thanks to the long spout, the water gets exactly where it is needed.
127726.m: You water plants with a watering can.

127727.q: Why do you put a rose on the watering can?
a: So the water falls gently like rain
127727.e: A thick jet can wash soil away and bend delicate plants over. With the rose, the water falls gently.
127727.m: With the rose, plants get gentle rain.

127728.q: Why does the spout of a watering can reach as high as the can itself?
a: Otherwise water would run out of the front when filling
So it is easier to carry
127728.e: The can and the spout are connected at the bottom, so the water stands at the same height in both. If the spout were shorter, the water would spill out of the front.
127728.m: The spout must be as high as the can.

127729.q: What do you have to do to make water flow out of the watering can?
a: Put the can in the sun
127729.e: When you tip it, the opening of the spout is lower than the water in the can. Then the water flows out.
127729.m: If you tip the can, the water flows out.

127730.q: When is the best time to water plants in summer?
a: In the morning or the evening
Only at night during a storm
127730.e: In the midday heat, a lot of water evaporates before it reaches the roots. In the morning or evening, more water is left for the plants.
127730.m: In summer it is best to water in the morning or evening.

127731.q: What can block the small holes of a watering rose over time?
127731.e: Tap water contains dissolved lime. When the water dries, the lime is left behind and clogs the holes.
127731.m: Limescale can block the holes of a rose.

127732.q: What happens if you tip a full watering can too far?
a: Water also runs out of the filling hole at the top
The water flows back into the can
No water comes out at all
127732.e: If you tip it a lot, the big opening at the top is also lower than the water. Then water sloshes out there too.

127733.e: From a hydrant the fire brigade gets a lot of water quickly. They use it to put out fires.
127733.m: The fire brigade gets its water for putting out fires from hydrants.

127734.q: Where can you find lots of hydrants in Switzerland?
a: At the side of the road
127734.e: Hydrants stand along the roads in villages and towns. That way the fire brigade can reach them quickly.
127734.m: Hydrants stand at the side of the road.

127735.q: What is a hydrant connected to?
a: The water main under the road
127735.e: The pipes of the water supply run under the road. The hydrant is connected to these pipes.
127735.m: A hydrant is connected to the water main.

127736.q: What does the fire brigade connect to a hydrant?
127736.e: Hydrants have connections for fire hoses. The water flows through the hoses to the fire.
127736.m: The fire brigade connects its hoses to the hydrant.

127737.q: Not all hydrants can be seen above the ground. Where are the others?
a: Under a cover in the ground
127737.e: These hydrants are called underground hydrants. They are under a cover in the road or the pavement.
127737.m: Some hydrants are under a cover in the ground.

127738.q: Why must you not park a car in front of a hydrant?
a: The fire brigade must be able to reach it quickly
127738.e: In a fire, every minute counts. A parked car could block the hydrant.
127738.m: There must always be space in front of hydrants.

127739.q: Why does the water come out of a hydrant with a lot of pressure?
a: Because it comes from stores high up
127739.e: The water stores are usually higher than the houses. So the water pushes hard through the pipes.
127739.m: Stores high up give the hydrant pressure.

127740.q: What does the fire brigade use to open a hydrant?
127740.e: The hydrant key fits exactly onto the hydrant's valve. You use it to turn it on and off.
127740.m: You open a hydrant with a hydrant key.

127741.q: What does a water pump do?
127741.e: A pump pushes or sucks water through pipes. This way water can also go upwards or a long way.
127741.m: A pump moves water to where it is needed.

127742.q: What is the old hand pump with a long lever at a well called?
127742.e: The long lever is the pump handle. If you move it up and down, water comes out of the pipe.
127742.m: With a lever hand pump, you pump with a long lever.

127743.q: After a storm there is water in the cellar. How can a pump help?
127743.e: The pump sucks up the water from the cellar floor. It pushes it outside through a hose.
127743.m: A pump can get water out of a cellar.

127744.q: What is a pump called that you lower completely into the water of a well?
127744.e: A submersible pump works under water. It pushes the water up through a pipe.
127744.m: A submersible pump works under water.

127745.q: Which very old invention lifts water upwards with a turning screw?
127745.e: A large screw turns inside a tube. With every turn, a little water is pushed further up.
127745.m: Archimedes' screw lifts water by turning.

127746.q: What drives most water pumps today?
127746.e: Today most pumps run on electricity. In the past, muscle power or water wheels were needed.
127746.m: Most pumps run on electricity today.

127747.q: Why does a car with a petrol engine have a water pump?
a: It pumps cooling water through the engine
It fills petrol into the tank
127747.e: An engine gets very hot while driving. The cooling water takes up the heat and protects it from overheating.
127747.m: The water pump keeps the car engine cool.

127748.q: What does the pump in an aquarium do?
a: It moves the water through a filter
127748.e: The pump sucks in water and pushes it through a filter. This keeps the water clean and moving.
127748.m: In an aquarium, the pump keeps the water clean.

127749.q: What do you need a spirit level for?
a: To check whether something is straight
127749.e: With a spirit level you can see whether a shelf or a picture is crooked. In German it is called a ‘water scale’, but it doesn't weigh anything.
127749.m: A spirit level shows whether something is straight.

127750.q: What can you see in the little tube of a spirit level?
127750.e: The tube contains a liquid with a small air bubble. You read from the bubble whether something is straight.
127750.m: The air bubble in a spirit level shows the position.

127751.q: Where is the bubble when the spirit level is perfectly horizontal?
a: Exactly in the middle between the lines
Right at the left of the tube
Right at the right of the tube
At the bottom of the tube
127751.e: The tube is slightly curved. When the level is straight, the highest point is in the middle, and that is where the bubble sits.
127751.m: If the bubble is in the middle, everything is level.

127752.q: Why does the air bubble always move to the highest point in the tube?
a: Air is lighter than the liquid
Air is heavier than the liquid
The bubble sticks to the glass
127752.e: The heavy liquid sinks and pushes the light air upwards. So the bubble always shows the highest point.
127752.m: Light air rises in a liquid.

127753.q: Why does the tube of a spirit level often contain a liquid with alcohol rather than pure water?
a: So it doesn't freeze in winter
So it glows in the dark
127753.e: Pure water would turn to ice in frost. The liquid with alcohol stays liquid even in the cold.
127753.m: Alcohol in the tube protects the spirit level from frost.

127754.q: What is the little tube with the bubble in a spirit level called?
127754.e: The tube is called a vial. In German it has the same name as the insect dragonfly. Some spirit levels have several vials.
127754.m: The tube of a spirit level is called a vial.

127755.q: Who often needs a spirit level at work?
127755.e: Bricklayers and carpenters have to build walls, floors and furniture straight. The spirit level helps them do that.
127755.m: Builders use a spirit level to build straight.

127756.q: A spirit level also has a tube fitted crossways. What is it for?
a: To check whether something is upright
127756.e: If you hold the level against a door frame, the crossways tube shows whether it is vertical. You can also check posts and walls this way.
127756.m: With the crossways tube you check whether something is vertical.

127757.q: What do you often feel in your ears when you dive deep?
127757.e: The water pushes against the ear from outside. That feels like pressure or a slight pain.
127757.m: When diving you feel the water pressure in your ears.

127758.q: What is it called when divers even out the pressure in their ears?
127758.e: When equalising, the pressure inside the ear becomes the same as outside. Then the unpleasant pressure stops.
127758.m: Equalising makes the pressure inside and outside the same.

127759.q: What is the thin skin in the ear called that bends inwards when you dive?
127759.e: The eardrum separates the ear canal from the middle ear. It is as thin as the skin on a drum.
127759.m: The eardrum is a thin skin in the ear.

127760.q: What can help the pressure in your ears to ease?
127760.e: When you swallow, a passage between the throat and the ear opens briefly. Then air can get in and the pressure is evened out.
127760.m: Swallowing helps even out the pressure in your ears.

127761.q: What do many divers do with their nose when equalising?
a: They pinch it and blow gently
127761.e: With the nose pinched, the air pushes gently into the ears. So the pressure inside becomes the same as outside.
127761.m: Pinching your nose and blowing gently evens out the pressure.

127762.q: Where else do people often feel the same pressure in their ears?
127762.e: When landing, the air pressure in the cabin rises. That also pushes on the eardrum.
127762.m: In a plane you also need to even out the pressure in your ears.

127763.q: Why shouldn't you dive with a bad cold?
127763.e: With a cold, the nose and the passages to the ear are often blocked. Then no air can get into the ear, and diving hurts.
127763.m: With a blocked nose, equalising works badly.

127764.q: What should you do if your ears hurt while diving?
a: Slowly swim a bit higher again
127764.e: Pain is a warning sign. Higher up the pressure is lower, and the ear is spared.
127764.m: If your ears hurt, don't dive deeper.

127765.q: When should you equalise while diving down?
127765.e: With every metre of depth the pressure gets bigger. If you equalise early and often, you hardly feel any pain.
127765.m: Equalising early and often protects your ears.

127766.q: What does the abbreviation HTML stand for?
127766.e: Written out, HTML means Hypertext Markup Language. With HTML you describe how web pages are built up.
127766.m: HTML is the basis from which web pages are built.

127767.q: What kind of language is HTML?
127767.e: With HTML you mark up content, for example: this is a heading, this is a paragraph. There are no loops or calculations in HTML as there are in a programming language.
127767.m: HTML describes the structure of a page, but it does not calculate anything.

127768.e: The British physicist Tim Berners-Lee developed HTML together with the World Wide Web. At the time he was working at the CERN research centre.
127768.m: Tim Berners-Lee is considered the inventor of HTML and the World Wide Web.

127769.q: What goes between <body> and </body> in an HTML document?
a: The visible content of the page
127769.e: Everything in the body element is shown by the browser in the window. This includes texts, pictures, links and forms.
127769.m: What is in the body is what you see on the web page.

127770.q: Which file extension does a typical HTML file have?
127770.e: HTML files usually end in .html, sometimes also .htm. The home page of a website is often called index.html.
127770.m: You can recognise an HTML file by the extension .html.

127771.q: Which line does a modern HTML5 document usually begin with?
127771.e: The line <!DOCTYPE html> tells the browser that it is an HTML5 document. It goes right at the start of the file.
127771.m: An HTML5 document begins with <!DOCTYPE html>.

127772.q: Which program is enough for writing HTML code?
127772.e: HTML is plain text. So you can write it in any simple text editor and save it as an .html file.
127772.m: A simple text editor is enough for HTML.

127773.q: What is the content between <head> and </head> in an HTML document called?
127773.e: The head section contains information about the page, for example the title and the character encoding. This information is usually not shown directly on the page.
127773.m: The head section contains information about the page, not the visible content.

127774.q: What is CSS responsible for on a web page?
127774.e: With CSS you set colours, fonts, spacing and the layout. HTML supplies the structure, CSS the design.
127774.m: CSS decides how a web page looks.

127775.q: What does the abbreviation CSS stand for?
127775.e: CSS means Cascading Style Sheets. Cascading means that several rules work together according to a fixed order of priority.
127775.m: CSS are design rules that work according to an order of priority.

127776.q: Which CSS property changes the text colour?
127776.e: The property color sets the font colour, for example color: red. The other properties control alignment, spacing and borders.
127776.m: In CSS you set the text colour with color.

127777.q: Which CSS property sets the background colour?
127777.e: With background-color you colour the background of an element. There is no property called text-color in CSS.
127777.m: You colour the background with background-color.

127778.q: What do you use a class such as .important for in CSS?
a: To give many elements the same design
To make the page load faster
127778.e: A class selector such as .important targets all elements with class="important". This way you design many elements with a single rule.
127778.m: In CSS you write classes with a full stop in front.

127779.q: How often should an ID such as id="title" appear on a web page?
127779.e: An ID is like a name that belongs to only one element. In CSS you target it with a hash sign, for example #title.
127779.m: In CSS you select an ID with the hash sign.

127780.q: Which CSS property changes the font size?
127780.e: With font-size you set how big a text appears, for example font-size: 20px. The other names are not valid CSS properties.
127780.m: You set the font size with font-size.

127781.q: What is the difference between margin and padding in CSS?
a: margin is the outer spacing, padding the inner spacing
margin is the colour, padding the font
margin is the border, padding the shadow
margin only applies to pictures, padding only to text
127781.e: In the box model, padding lies between the content and the border, margin outside the border. This lets you control spacing exactly.
127781.m: Padding is inside, margin is outside.

127782.q: Where do you usually include an external CSS file in the HTML page?
a: In the head section with the link element
Right at the end in the footer element
127782.e: With <link rel="stylesheet" href="style.css"> in the head section a CSS file is loaded. This way the design applies to the whole page.
127782.m: You link a CSS file in the head section with the link element.

127783.q: Which HTML element makes the largest heading?
127783.e: Headings go from <h1> to <h6>, with <h1> being the most important and largest. <h6> is the smallest level.
127783.m: The most important heading on a page goes in h1.

127784.q: Which HTML element stands for a paragraph of text?
127784.e:
The p stands for paragraph. The text goes between

and

.
127784.m: In HTML a paragraph is marked up with p.

127785.q: Which HTML element do you use to include a picture?
127785.e: The element shows a picture; you give the picture file in the src attribute. It needs no closing tag.
127785.m: In HTML you include pictures with img.

127786.q: Which attribute of describes the picture in words for people who cannot see it?
127786.e: The alternative text in the alt attribute is read aloud by screen readers, for example. It also appears if the picture cannot be loaded.
127786.m: Every picture needs a descriptive alt text.

127787.q: Which HTML element creates an unordered list with bullet points?
127787.e: ul stands for unordered list. The individual entries each go in <li> elements.
127787.m: A list with bullet points begins with ul.

127788.q: Which HTML element do you use for a numbered list?
127788.e: ol stands for ordered list. The browser numbers the entries automatically.
127788.m: You write a numbered list with ol.

127789.e: stands for break and starts a new line without starting a new paragraph. It has no closing tag.
127789.m: With br you force a line break.

127790.q:
